en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on King Ajātaśatru, Volume One.
Translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Lokakṣema of the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with twelve thousand [monks].

Accompanied by one thousand bhikṣus and eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas—each one more venerable than the next—all these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had attained all the dhāraṇīs, had attained unimpeded resolve, and had attained the state of non-arising dharmas; they possessed such samādhi-wisdom that they fully knew the mental activities of all people's hearts and, according to their inclinations, taught them the Dharma so that each might attain their proper place.
The Four Great Kings and Śakra, Lord of Devas, as well as the devaputras, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, all came to the assembly.
At that time, Mañjuśrī was on a different part of the mountain, together with twenty-five superior persons.
Who were these twenty-five? They were all bodhisattvas, each having their own name, namely:
Narasiri, Naradashiri, Sambasiri, Kapphatasiri,
Phatutasiri, Kajasindhalu, Dharanidhalu, Radhabhani, Radhamahata, Sihakama, and Sihakavijaya.
Kulakāñcana-ja, sahacittopala, macaka-pauṣkara-candana,
hāridra, tīrṇa-kūṭa-śarkara, mahā-mṛdvīka, acchānanda, piṅgala-mañjiṣṭha, rājānanda.
Dharmatrāta, Ghosaka, Vasumitra, Buddhadeva, Parśva, Ksanti, Ghoṣila, Buddharakṣa, Saṃgharakṣa, Mātr̥ceṭa, Kumāralāta, Sthiramati, Guṇamati, Vimalamitra, Prajñāgupta, Guṇaprabha, Śrīlāta,
Dharmatrāta, Arambhivila, Matṛtaśa, Mukatita, and Ajudhasahrasravas— these are the names of the twenty-five eminent masters.

Four devaputras from the Tuṣita heaven came to where Mañjuśrī was, desiring to hear the Dharma; their names were Samantakusuma, Aniketa, Manojñagandhaśāha, and Utsadavigha—these were the four devaputras.
Furthermore, there were a few other devaputras who came to where Mañjuśrī was in order to listen to the Dharma.

Once these noble beings and all the devaputras were seated, each spoke of the Buddha’s wisdom as being most sublime, infinite, inconceivable, immeasurable, and unfathomable; it cannot be matched by the vows of ordinary persons. They all said:
"By what practice and through what skillful means can one realize the ultimate wisdom, even unto the inconceivable omniscience of a Buddha?"
The Bodhisattva Wisdom Chief said:
"One who never tires of merit and harbors no expectations regarding any merits may attain infinite wisdom."
The Bodhisattva Huishi said:

"When the mind is equanimous and tranquil, when that mind is joyful and supple, and one follows its instructions, one then maintains the mind of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) and becomes firm in saṃnāha-saṃnaddha (the great armor). One who acts in this way may reach infinite wisdom."
The Bodhisattva Paripūrṇasamatā said:
"Not calculating the number of kalpas—such that the incalculable future kalpas cannot be reckoned—is what constitutes saṃnāha."
"One who does not harbor self-conceit regarding their vows (saṃnāha) may reach ultimate wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Sampannacaryā said:
"One who does not harbor thoughts of personal security may reach ultimate wisdom."
Why is this? It is because one desires to bring peace and security to all.
One who forms such a thought does not seek anything for themselves other than the complete peace and security of all; such a person may attain infinite wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Padmavyūha said:
"One who cannot subdue their own mind cannot subdue the minds of others.
Only one who can subdue their own mind can subdue the minds of others; by acting in this way, one may attain infinite wisdom."
The Bodhisattva Padmacaryakalpa said:
"Those who follow desire cannot transcend desire; those who do not follow desire are the ones who transcend desire."

As for that bodhisattva, whether gain or loss is obtained, his mind remains without distinction; whether there is suffering or pleasure, slander or praise, evil or goodness, he is unattached to any of these.
Why is this? Because one neither grieves nor rejoices.
One who acts in this manner may attain ultimate wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Restraining the Sense Faculties said:
"One should not think that one can obtain merit by observing the merits performed by others; whoever acts in this way does not enter into infinite wisdom."
One should contemplate solitude and the absence of companions. Why is this?
Because one contemplates all beings.
"Whatever remains unaccomplished, I shall accomplish it; with momentary diligence and without indolence, I desire to instruct all beings.
One who acts thus may reach infinite wisdom."
The Bodhisattva Earth-like Conduct said:
"It is like the earth: all grasses, trees, medicinal herbs, houses, and cities dwell upon the earth, yet the earth itself has no place where it dwells."
All beings depend on it for their livelihood, yet it does not consider this a burden.

A bodhisattva should likewise maintain such a mind: they should be like the earth, maintaining a mind free from both joy and anger, ensuring that all beings each find their proper place, without thinking of receiving anything in return.
"One who acts in this manner may attain boundless wisdom.
Bodhisattva Ratnapraṇidhi said:
"One should maintain a mind like that of a venerable one and not be self-deprecating; even in dreams, there should be no dualistic mind."
Why is this? Because they harbor no thoughts of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.

Whatever they do is like a jewel that never leaves the Bodhisattva; if they do not lose the hearts of all people, they have no greed or attachment toward precious jewels, and those who come to seek them, they all guide toward the Mahāyāna.

Why is this? Because there is no mind that is equal to the mind, and no wisdom of non-mind that is equal to this wisdom of mind; furthermore, there is neither increase nor decrease, and that mind is free from all craving or attachment.
"One who acts in this way may attain infinite wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta said:

"To view those in the cycle of birth and death within the five realms as if they had fallen into the sea, and for a bodhisattva to then feel compassion for them in his heart and reach out his hand to take hold of them—this is what must be done."

Why is this? It is because for those who lack wisdom, he acts as the head of wisdom; for those who are greedy, he acts as the head of non-attachment; for those who do not uphold the precepts, he acts as the head of morality; for those who are wrathful, he acts as the head of patience; for those who are indolent, he acts as the head of diligence; for those with distracted minds, he acts as the head of single-mindedness; for those who lack wisdom, he acts as the head of wisdom; for those who lack merit, he acts as the head of merit—sealing these with the head of merit, which is the Three Jewels of the Dharma.
What are the three?

To bring all beings to fulfillment by means of the Buddha’s wisdom through teaching and transformation; to personally realize the precious merits of one's own body; and to contemplate all dharmas as being like space. Therefore, these are the foremost among the treasures of the Dharma—these are the three.
"One who acts in this way may attain boundless wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Siṃhamati said:
"One whose body undertakes such saṃnāha (armor/vow) has nothing to fear and is not afraid; they neither retreat nor take off their robes, and the hair on their body does not stand on end."
Why is this? Because there is no evil within saṃsāra. Nor does one construct nirvāṇa;
abiding equally in suffering and pleasure, one does not give rise to dualistic thoughts.
"One who acts in this way may attain ultimate wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Fearless One Who Transcends with the Lion’s Gait said:
"Those who are weak and inferior cannot reach this; this is the deed of a Mahāsattva."

Why is this? Because by abandoning all evils, by being free from flattery and deceit, and by responding with sincerity and simplicity, one will not be arrogant, will have no mind of anger, and one's actions will not follow what is contrary to the Dharma.

Why is this so? Because through loyal governance, there is no lust or envy; because there is no evil mind, one's ignorance is like darkness [dispelled]; and because these are absent, one's body, speech, and mind are equal. What one says accords with what is said, and one does not lose the intended meaning; thus, whatever noble deeds one undertakes, they are brought to fulfillment.
Why is this? Because through supreme sincerity, they both find delight in the Dharma itself.
One who acts in accordance with the Dharma does not cling to or begrudge their own life.
Why is this? Because they do not cling to their own bodies or lives, nor do they abandon anything.
In what they bestow, they have no greed or regret, desiring only that people may find their proper place.
That which is entered correctly is not a deviant path. For those who are poor, he acts as a treasury of precious jewels;

for those who are ill, he acts as a physician; for those who are fearful, he acts as a protector; for those who are inferior, he acts as a ground of the Path; for those who have entered onto deviant paths, he acts as a righteous guide; for those who lack wisdom, he acts as wisdom. In all these instances of compliance, what cause for resentment could there be to give rise to such thoughts?
The Great Being, by means of this patience for deliverance within [this state], abides as he is in the fundamental nature of all dharmas.
One who acts thus reaches even unto ultimate wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Purple-Golden Color (Cāmikara-varṇa) said:
"His thoughts are like space.
Why is this? Because there is nowhere they do not pervade."

With great compassion that covers all without exception, his mind is ever joyful and his countenance is serene. His mind does not dwell upon any worldly pleasures or desires; his giving is like the heavens, which provide shelter for all. His precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom are likewise so.
"One who acts in this way may reach ultimate wisdom.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva Turning the Wheel of Dharma as soon as the Thought Aroused spoke:

"Those who have newly aroused the thought [of enlightenment] should not allow Māra to find an opportunity; they must not lose the intent of the Buddhas and celestial deities. Those who establish their minds in this way will correspond to the turning of the wheel of Dharma."
Why is this? Because they have given rise to a wholesome mind. Why is this?
"All dharmas are unarisen;
one who acts in this manner may attain the ultimate wisdom.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Sarvavāk-svabhāva-praveśa:
"You should maintain a mind that enters into all things. Why is this?
All dharmas are naturally such that their essence is entirely empty; everything spoken is likewise empty, just as space enters into all things without exception."
A bodhisattva should likewise be thus: there is nothing their mind does not penetrate; whatever they do accords with their word; and there is nothing their wisdom does not understand.
One who acts in this manner may attain ultimate wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Anihitārāma said:
"All sounds are without sound; all voices are unobtainable. One who knows this neither rejoices, nor grieves, nor becomes indolent."
Why is this so? It is like Mount Sumeru, which remains unmoved even when struck by the wind.
Whether encountering pleasant sounds or unpleasant sounds, the mind of a bodhisattva neither feels joy nor experiences sorrow.
Why is this? Because there is nothing to which one is attached.
That which is without attachment is called the Buddha’s word.

If the teachings of other paths are all empty and non-existent, and one perceives that all conditioned desires and activities are subject to exhaustion, then by knowing this exhaustion, one does not become arrogant.
One who practices this Dharma will swiftly attain Buddhahood.
Sāgaramati Bodhisattva said:
"That mind should be like that which is received by the ocean—wisdom that is boundless.
It is, for example, like the ocean, which receives all streams and unites them into a single flavor."
The Bodhisattva unifies all that exists into a single dharma. Why is this?
Because it is subtle and wondrous.

It does not undergo transformation through the twelve links of dependent origination; even when contemplating the Dharma-body, it neither increases nor decreases, yet it performs meritorious deeds for the sake of all beings.
The merit thus performed is intended so that all may attain it—this is called inexhaustible merit.
One should protect [the mind] by neither clinging nor abandoning, restraining the body through the power of the mind; whatever actions are performed, they are all equal and without distinction.
Because one acts in this way, the one who gives rise to the wisdom of intention will fully attain the ultimate wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Mahāprabhāsa said:

“One should maintain the mind such that its wisdom and its radiance are like those of a Buddha; these are not the products of worldly people. When the mind practices this radiance, there is nothing it does not illuminate.”

Why is this? It is because he wishes to cause the world to know that these constitute the Dharma: his mind practices the light of giving, which shines everywhere; it practices the light of morality, which shines everywhere; and it fully practices patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, such that their radiance shines everywhere.
"One who acts in this way may reach infinite wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Jvalanaprabha said:

"Taking the mind of merit and wisdom as one's eye, whatever forms one perceives are pure and free from evil; it is the same for sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena. Thus, one purifies these six matters."
What are the six?
They are the eye, the ear, the nose, the mouth, the body, and the mind.
One does not find delight in whatever is agreeable therein, because the mind is pure.

Regarding all people whom he beholds, he desires that they all enter the Buddha-dharma; those who are not upright, he transforms by leading them with the Dharma. When others come to seek whatever good things he possesses, he has no sense of attachment or parsimony; once he has given them away, he never regrets it.
"One who acts in this way may reach the ultimate wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Kāmacintin said:
"Even if one is reviled or beaten, they do not give rise to anger, but contemplate only the Dharma."
With what [thought] does one contemplate the Dharma? What is it that is reviled?
What is it that is resented?
The same applies to being beaten and whipped.
Because there is nothing to be apprehended in internal emptiness and no doubt regarding external emptiness, one perceives nothing of the body within the body, nor does one perceive another.

Why is this? If someone asks for his hands or feet, he joyfully gives them; if someone wishes to take his head, his heart is all the more glad. If they ask for his city or precious treasures, he has no greed or regret regarding those who seek them. If they seek his wife or children, he immediately bestows them as a gift without any change of heart.

If, upon reciting this sutra, one attains joy from even a single chapter, one will not take pleasure in the delights of a Golden Wheel-Turning King; one will preach the Dharma for all people without seeking the status of a Śakra; one will aspire to cause even a single person to resolve to become a Bodhisattva rather than aspiring to be a Brahmā; and one will seek to behold the Buddha rather than coveting the treasures of the trichiliocosm.
"One who acts in this way is always free from indolence; with such joy, one may reach the ultimate wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Viewed Without Bottom said:
"To view all that exists as not being 'mine'—this is what I call non-indolence."
All buddha-fields are utterly pure; one does not dwell upon existence or non-existence.
When beholding the Buddhas, one does not conceive of them as forms to be sought. Why is this?
Because he employs the Dharma-body,
he regards the minds of all people and does not seek anything that belongs to others. Why is this?
When his eye of virtue attains purity, he then possesses the divine eye and the perfection of spiritual powers.
Having attained the eye of wisdom, he knows that there is nothing whatsoever to be craved; he then attains the Buddha-eye, fully endowed with the eighteen unique qualities.
"One who has attained the Dharma-eye is endowed with the ten powers; one who acts in accordance with *saṃnāhasaṃnaddha* (the armored resolve) shall reach infinite wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Acting Without Bottomless Practice said:
"All that is done is like that which is done by the *sarvajña* (the omniscient one)."
Why is this? Because there is no abiding; since there is no abiding, one merely contemplates all dharmas.
When a bodhisattva acts in this way, they do not rely on any favorable conditions—how could they fall?
Nor does one fall due to transgressions, nor does one fall due to the deeds of Māra. Why is this?

Because they do not abandon the Dharma, and because they do not commit what is contrary to the Dharma, they reach this state, thereby transcending the transgressions and the deeds of Māra that have been committed.
"One who responds in this manner may reach the wisdom that is without limit.
The Bodhisattva Śamathacitta said:
"All that exists is not received from others; by what one does, one immediately subdues all Māras."

Because one knows that there is nothing to be attained and nothing further to be done, and because knowing there is nothing further to be done brings about the subduing of the five aggregates; because knowing the five aggregates means there are no demonic activities, and because crossing beyond the realm of Māra means that one’s practice of the Middle Way is free from obscuration—a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has thus crossed beyond obscuration and acts in this manner shall reach unsurpassed wisdom.
The Bodhisattva who gives rise to regret regarding what has been done said:
"One regrets those actions performed with an unrighteous intent; as for those actions performed in accordance with the Dharma, one's mind remains unchanged. Why is this so? [Because]..."
One should always apply oneself single-mindedly to doing good; whatever one does with the body, one should not wish for others to find it unacceptable.
Whatever one does with speech or mind, one should not wish for others to find it unacceptable.
For those who possess sorrow and anxiety, one uses the vastness of the Dharma to cause them to be free from sorrow and anxiety.
One who acts in this manner is a bodhisattva-mahāsattva and shall attain ultimate wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Sarvapraṇidhānaprāpta said:

"For one who possesses such pure precepts, whatever they wish for will surely be attained. This is because one with such pure precepts no longer transgresses worldly conventions; and by not transgressing worldly conventions, they accord with the roots and forest of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, which are like sarvajñatā (all-knowledge)."
"Those who possess such pure precepts do not transgress the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
This is what constitutes the work performed by a bodhisattva mahāsattva to reach unsurpassed wisdom.
Thus spoke the Devaputra Samantapuṣpa.
"It is like a tree that has flowers; there is no one who beholds it who does not rejoice, and there is none among those who have performed meritorious deeds who does not benefit from it.
It is like the *kovidāra* tree in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, whose flowers bloom in profusion, and which all the devas cherish and delight in."
The Bodhisattva takes the Dharma as eyes for all beings; he is like a flower, or like a celestial maṇi-jewel free from blemish.
When a Bodhisattva purifies his mind in this way, one who acts thus may attain ultimate wisdom.
The Devaputra Prabhāsa-puṣpa said:
"It is like the rising of the sun: all darkness is utterly dispelled, and all forms become visible.
In the same way, the Bodhisattva, through wisdom, has nothing that it does not illuminate; thus, the darkness of all ignorance is completely exhausted and opened up."
Why is this? Because it will ultimately lead to illumination.
Those who dwell in darkness, upon seeing the light, immediately attain the path.
The Bodhisattva, by abiding upon the path, points out the way to those who have lost it.
By means of such a person, one may reach infinite wisdom.
The Devaputra Tianxianghua said:

"Just as the fragrance of the mandārava flower is perceived for forty li in every direction—across, up, down, and in the four intermediate quarters—so too, the Bodhisattva takes the pure precepts, samādhi, and the wisdom he has attained as his fragrance; there is no one throughout the trichiliocosm who does not perceive it."
This fragrance heals the illnesses of countless people through the pure precepts, samādhi, and wisdom they have heard.
When a bodhisattva abides in these, they shall attain ultimate wisdom.
The Devaputra Śraddhādharmapratipanna said:
"One who abides in the Dharma and acts accordingly, who, like a Bodhisattva, is never again indolent, has no further sloth, and is free from discursive thought, shall attain ten matters:

practicing the six pāramitās; employing the four immeasurable minds, the five phrases, and the four matters; encompassing the three liberations and the patience that benefits and inspires others to resolve their minds; never being separated from the body [of practice]; teaching through upāyakauśalya (skillful means); upholding all essential dharmas; and having no difference in what one believes. These are the ten matters."
"One who acts in this manner may reach infinite wisdom.
Mañjuśrī then addressed the noble persons and the devaputras:
"A bodhisattva dwells in non-dwelling."
What is meant by dwelling in non-dwelling?
It is not to take the three realms as a basis for practice; that which is not practiced is the internal, and that which seeks no further practice is the external.
Although externally they do not fall into the stage of the disciples and have nothing to practice, they likewise do not fall into the stage of the pratyekabuddhas.
"Practice" refers to birth and death; what is practiced and learned refers to the absence of anything known.
That which is practiced is "name"; that which is learned through practice is "form.
That which is practiced is "conditioned origination" (hetu-pratyaya); that which is learned through practice refers to "that which is seen.
That which is practiced is "craving" (tṛṣṇā); that which is learned through practice refers to "that which has roots."
What is practiced is called "self," while what is learned is called "not-self.
What is practiced is greed; what is learned is that there is no difference between what is given and the act of giving.
What is practiced is the violation of precepts; what is learned is not being conceited regarding one's own observance of the precepts.
Those who habitually harbor anger train themselves in patience without becoming conceited.
Those who habitually lack diligence train themselves in vigor without becoming self-conceited.
To practice means that when the mind is distracted, one trains to achieve single-mindedness without becoming conceited.
To practice means that when there is ignorance, one trains in wisdom without becoming conceited.
"Practice" refers to the absence of merit; "that which is practiced and learned" refers to performing meritorious deeds without arrogance.
"Practice" refers to worldly dharmas; "that which is practiced and learned" refers to the dharmas of the Path without self-exalting pride.
To practice means to be without liberation; that which is practiced and learned is to attain liberation while remaining free from arrogance.
To practice means to have faults; that which is practiced and learned is to be without faults and likewise free from arrogance.
To "practice" means that while there is still something remaining, one practices until there is nothing remaining left, yet remains free from arrogance.
The Bodhisattva practices without anything to practice; he protects all things, neither clinging to them nor abandoning them. One who acts in this way shall reach ultimate wisdom.
All dharmas are entirely unattainable. Why is this?
Because there is nothing into which they enter, nor is there anything into which they do not enter.
This omniscience leads directly to omniscience; that which is non-apprehensible is omniscience.
One cannot conceive of attaining omniscience by means of form (*rūpa*); it is the same for sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
It does not follow from the category of dharmas, nor does it follow from the category of non-dharmas;
nor is it reckoned as the gift of omniscience.
Why is this? Because the giver is likewise not separate from omniscience.
Morality, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom are also not to be reckoned as such.
Why is this? Because all-knowledge arises from wisdom.
The Omniscient One enters into nothing, yet he does not transcend the past or the future, nor does he enter the present.
Why is this? Because he has transcended the three periods of time.
The Omniscient One does not view with the eye; it is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. Why is this?
Because he has transcended all realms.
If men or women desire to seek omniscience, they should abide as one who abides in omniscience.
How should they abide?
By not abiding anywhere at all in regard to all phenomena; this is what it means to abide in omniscience.
Not conceiving of dharmas as "mine," one who acts in this way possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
All persons, dharmas, and Buddha-dharmas are thus without distinction; this is what constitutes all-knowledge.
Those who seek to attain all-knowledge must ultimately do so by means of the four great elements. Why is this?
Because they do not conceive of the body as a self.
Why is this? It is because it does not function by way of causal conditions.

Whether there are dharmas of merit or dharmas without merit, whatever is considered "mine" is not mine; that which is "I" is unborn, and that which is unborn has no conceptualization. Such conceptualization is itself non-arising, and what is shown or seen is entirely without birth. By means of the wisdom that knows non-birth and the unborn, to act in such a manner is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).

When Mañjuśrī had spoken these words, two thousand devaputras all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and twelve thousand people all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, equal path of enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva Anihata-rati addressed Mañjuśrī, saying, "Let us go together to the place where the Buddha is, to ask how a bodhisattva should abide.
At that moment, Mañjuśrī manifested a transformation-body Tathāgata who sat within the assembly; his form and attire were identical to those of Śākyamuni Buddha.
Mañjuśrī addressed the bodhisattva Padmottara, saying:
"Regarding what you have just asked, the Buddha is present here; you may now ask about the dwelling of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Pṛthivīkūṭa did not know that this was a manifested Buddha, so he knelt before him and asked:
"Tathāgata! How should a bodhisattva abide?"
The emanated Buddha said,
"As I have acted, so should a bodhisattva abide.
He asked again:
"How is it that one is like a Buddha? The Buddha said:

"It is neither through giving, nor through precepts, patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom; neither through desire, nor through form, nor through the formless; neither through bodily conduct, nor through verbal conduct, nor through mental conduct—because all such practices are without attachment."
That Buddha asked Pāṭibhānakulī,
"Does that which is transformed have a source from which it proceeds? He replied:
"There is no place from which one proceeds.
That Buddha said:
"Just as a magical creation has no place from which it proceeds, so should a bodhisattva practice."
The Bodhisattva Pṛthivīkūṭa again asked Mañjuśrī:
"Will this Buddha have no emanation-buddhas? Mañjuśrī replied:
"If you know for yourself that all phenomena are like illusions? he replied,
"All phenomena are indeed like illusions."
Mañjuśrī said: "Since one already knows that all phenomena are transformations, why ask again about the transformation of the Tathāgata? Mañjuśrī continued:
“Virtuous one, do you mean that all Buddhas are transformations?
He then asked Mañjuśrī again:
“From what are the Buddhas transformed?”
Mañjuśrī said: "Since that which is created is fundamentally pure, for what reason is there transformation? Mañjuśrī continued:
"Therefore, the Buddha has no self, no person, no life-principle, and no vital force; he does not abide by means of the Buddha, nor does he abide by means of ordinary people."
The Bodhisattva Pṛthu-kauṣṭhila again asked the transformation Buddha:
"What did you originally study to have attained Buddhahood for yourself?
That Buddha replied:
“Non-learning is the training of a bodhisattva. Why is this?

Because they do not think to themselves, ‘I wish to seek this,’ nor do they think, ‘I do not seek this. They neither grieve nor rejoice; they do not take conditions as objects, nor are they transformed by them. There is nothing seen and no location; there is no perception and no name; there is no form. To have no expectations whatsoever regarding anything—this is the training of a bodhisattva.”

One who trains in this manner trains in equality; one who trains in this manner is without attachment and without bondage; one who trains in this manner is without desire, without anger, and without delusion; one who trains in this manner is without love and without hatred. One who trains in this way does not think to themselves, "I am training in this"; such is the training in training in this way.
"One who trains in this manner does not fall into the evil realms.
That Buddha said:
"If there are those who seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and desire to achieve the state of a Buddha, they should train as I have trained."
He asked again:
"What is the study of the Buddha?
That Buddha replied:

“Neither committing offenses nor falling into offenses, neither giving nor grasping; neither holding nor not holding; neither observing precepts nor having precepts; neither practicing patience nor harboring malice; neither exerting diligence nor being indolent; neither practicing meditation nor having a distracted mind; neither possessing wisdom nor having anything known; neither having anything to learn nor not having anything to learn; neither achieving anything nor having anything achieved; neither being a bodhisattva nor being the Buddha-dharma; neither conceiving the thought that one has a body nor conceiving the thought that others have bodies.”

That which is seen is without conceptualization; it is neither the conceptualization of dharmas nor the conceptualization of non-dharmas, nor is it the conceptualization of neither-conceptualization-nor-non-conceptualization.
The Buddha said:
“One who understands this, a bodhisattva should train in this way.”
Why is this so? Because all phenomena have the characteristic of being like an illusion;
all phenomena are entirely joined together.
Why is this so? Although there are immeasurable things, when one contemplates them, they are all empty; because nothing exists, their conjunction is emptiness.
All phenomena are invisible.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are equal and without distinction;
all dharmas are utterly silent.
Why is this? Because it is neither spoken nor uttered;
therefore, it has no location.
Why is this? Because all dharmas are unarisen.
One who believes this does not dwell on what is practiced, nor does he dwell on liberation, nor does the bodhisattva harbor self-conceit.
That Buddha said:
"If one hears this teaching and is neither terrified, nor frightened, nor afraid, for this reason they are called a bodhisattva.
It is like space, which is not afraid of fire, not afraid of wind, not afraid of rain, not afraid of smoke, not afraid of clouds, and likewise not afraid of thunder or lightning."
Why is this? Because these are empty dharmas.
A bodhisattva should be thus: entirely without fear or dread.
"When the Bodhisattva’s mind is like space, he then subdues all Māras; he can then become a Buddha and act as a protector for all beings.
Having finished speaking these words, the emanated Buddha vanished once more.
The Bodhisattva Pṛthivīkūṭa asked Mañjuśrī,
"Where is the Tathāgata now heading? He replied:
"From where it comes, there it converges; from where it converges, it comes.
Bodhisattva Paṭipāṇikūli said to Mañjuśrī:
"That which is an emanation comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; what, then, does it mean to 'come from'?"
Mañjuśrī replied:
"It is like a magical creation: it comes without a path and goes without a path.
All phenomena are likewise; they come from nowhere and go nowhere."
Pārṣṇika further asked:
"What is the locus of all dharmas?
He then replied:
"He naturally abides in this state.
He asked again:
"What is the state wherein all things abide?"
"Its 'place' is that which is performed.
He asked again:
"All phenomena are without performance and without fault."
Mañjuśrī said: “In this way, all dharmas are without action and without fault.
When those dharmas pass away, there is neither an agent nor one who commits a fault; everything that exists is entirely subsumed within the Dharmakāya.”
He then asked Mañjuśrī again:
“If there is no agent and no offense, why do you say that people follow what they have done? Mañjuśrī replied:
"It is exactly as you have asked: a person neither acts nor incurs guilt. Why is this?
Because this person is the Dharma-body of dharmas, they neither act nor incur guilt; what is done, what is attained, and these three are equal."
The Bodhisattva Parivartakuli asked again:
"Are these three things equal? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Because the Tathāgatas are equal, these three matters are likewise equal.
He asked again:
“The Tathāgata is without action, without transgression, and without attainment; by what cause are these three matters equal?”
Mañjuśrī said: "The Tathāgata is without action, without transgression, and without attainment.
His actions, his transgressions, and his attainments are equal because they accord with what is done."
"Those transgressions have already passed and the offenses are no longer seen; because they have passed, even in the future they shall not depart from the Tathāgata—thus it is said.

At that time, as if in the presence of Śākyamuni Buddha, the Venerable Śāriputra, Ānanda, and all the venerable bhikṣus, through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, heard everything that Mañjuśrī had spoken.
Śāriputra said:
"Excellent, excellent!

The deeds performed by this superior person move all things through the Dharma; he does not depart from the Dharmakāya. When those with wisdom hear this, there are none who do not resolve to attain enlightenment."
The Buddha said:
“It is exactly as you have said.
A bodhisattva trains in that which is not to be trained; what they speak is equal and without distinction, just as one reaps the fruit according to what was sown.”
"The wisdom that a bodhisattva studies is such that what is spoken is identical to wisdom.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"If you study in this manner, you will personally attain this wisdom."
The Bodhisattva Light from the Crown addressed the Buddha:
“What is that which is studied by the śrāvakas?
What is that which is studied by the bodhisattvas?”
The Buddha said:
"To train as a disciple is because there are limits and attachments; for a bodhisattva to train is to be without limits and without obstructions.
Thus, those who are śrāvakas have a small training and little wisdom."
“A Bodhisattva trains in the vast; that which he knows is without limit, and that which he speaks is free from all obstruction.
The Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha addressed the Buddha:
“May the Tathāgata manifest his spiritual resonance, causing the assembly of Mañjuśrī to all come here.”
Why is this? It is so that all those present in this assembly may attain that which is without loss. Why is this?
"What Mañjuśrī has spoken is profoundly deep and subtle.
Those who wish to hear it shall each attain their own place according to their desires.

The Buddha was immediately moved; at that moment, Mañjuśrī, together with twenty-five superior persons and various devaputras, arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated before him, and stood respectfully.
The Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha asked Mañjuśrī, “The Buddha is here;
by what cause and condition does he preach the Dharma while being in another place?
Mañjuśrī replied:

"The reason I am not among them is that the Buddha is most venerable and cannot be confronted; whether what is said accords with the Tathāgata’s intention or does not, it is for this reason that I remain to one side."
That bodhisattva asked again:
"What dharma must be taught so that one may become a Tathāgata?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"The Buddha knows this himself.
He spoke again:
"Even so, you must explain its meaning."
Mañjuśrī then said: "I shall speak briefly according to what I know.
He then spoke:
"What do you mean by 'this'?
Mañjuśrī replied, "As it has been taught,
the Dharma that is taught is not different [from that teaching]."
As with the Tathāgata, he is like the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and is ineffable; he dwells according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Dharma.

For the sake of the Tathāgata’s intention, he has no place of rest and no place of cessation; he neither relies nor has anything to rely upon; there is neither increase nor decrease. Speaking in this way, he does not lose the Tathāgata’s intention; he loses nothing of his own person, nor does he cause others to lose anything; he does not lose the Dharma, nor does he lose saṃsāra, nor does he lose nirvāṇa. One who speaks in this manner does not lose the Tathāgata’s intention.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is just as Mañjuśrī has spoken; it accords with the intention of the Tathāgata.”
Why is this? Because it neither exceeds nor diminishes;
it is precisely the middle, free from all conceptualization.
Why is this? Mañjuśrī, when he speaks of matters while in the worldly samādhi, it remains as it was; he does not perceive any phenomenon that increases or any that decreases.
"As Mañjuśrī has spoken, he does not lose the intent of the Tathāgata.
When these words were spoken, eight hundred devaputras all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

At that time, there were also two hundred devaputras within the assembly who had previously resolved their minds on awakening but whose resolve was not yet firm; they were all on the verge of falling back and each had this thought:
"The Buddha-dharma is boundless, and it is difficult to attain Buddhahood."
"We do not abide in the training of a bodhisattva; it would be better for us to attain parinirvāṇa as arhats or pratyekabuddhas.

The Buddha, knowing fully that these people were capable of becoming bodhisattvas but had temporarily turned their minds away from that intent, then manifested himself as a householder (gṛhapati). Carrying a bowl filled with food of a hundred flavors, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated before him, and offered the bowl to the Buddha, saying:
"Please, out of compassion, accept this."
The Buddha then accepted the bowl.
Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"Even as you eat, you should remember your former kindness."
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"From what basis did the Buddha originally [teach], such that Mañjuśrī says one should mind one's old kindness?
He then asked the Buddha:
“Mañjuśrī, by virtue of what original merit has he been established as a Tathāgata?
The Buddha said, “Be patient for a moment; I shall now resolve your doubts for you.”

He immediately set the bowl down upon the ground, and the bowl descended, passing through various Buddha-fields. It went straight down past as many fields as there are grains of sand in seventy-two Ganges Rivers. Those fields are named *Ukhasa*; *Ukhasa* is a term from the language of India, which in the Han language means "Bright Opening. The Buddha there is named *Tāpilaraya*, which in the Han language means "King of Radiance," and he currently resides there.
That bowl remained suspended in the air within that buddha-field, and there was no one to hold it.
As the bowl passed through various buddha-fields, the attendant of each Buddha asked his own Buddha:
"From where has this bowl come?"
The Buddhas said:
"In the direction above, there is a land called Sahā, where the Buddha is named Śākyamuni; the bowl has come from there. Why is this so?"
"Because he intends to rescue and protect those bodhisattvas who have fallen away, he has moved them through his transformations.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Go and seek out the bowl and bring it here."

Śāriputra, immediately receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, entered ten thousand samādhis by means of his own power of wisdom; yet he neither saw nor attained anything beyond ten thousand buddha-fields.
Emerging from samādhi, he reported to the Buddha:
"I sought it but did not see it; I could not find it.
The Buddha said:
"Let it be; set it aside.
The Buddha spoke again to Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Go and seek out the bowl."

Then, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and personally endowed with the strength of his supernormal powers, he entered eight thousand samādhis and traversed eight thousand buddha-fields, yet saw nothing and attained nothing.
Then, emerging from samādhi, he returned to inform the Buddha:
"I sought it but did not see it; I could not obtain it.
The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"Go and seek out a bowl.
He then entered twelve thousand samādhis and traveled across twelve thousand Buddha-fields, yet he neither saw nor obtained one.
He immediately emerged from samādhi and returned to inform the Buddha:
"Though one seeks it and does not see it, one cannot obtain it.
Thus, the five hundred venerable bhikṣus each used their supernormal powers to search for the bowl, yet they could neither see it nor obtain it.
Subhūti rose from his seat and addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva:
"Virtuous One, you are of lofty talent, a successor in this very life who manifests as a future Buddha.
While we have traveled seeking the bowl but were unable to find it, we pray that you will go and seek it."
Maitreya then replied:

"If what you have said is true—that I am indeed one who is to be reborn in this very life for final enlightenment—then I do not equal Mañjuśrī regarding the samādhi he has attained, nor even its name."
Listen to what I say:

when I become a Buddha, even if there were as many people as the sands of the Ganges River, all becoming Mañjuśrīs, they still would not be able to know the matters of my walking—how I lift my feet and set them down;
they truly cannot reach it, just as they do not now.
"It would be better to seek it by repaying Mañjuśrī.
Then Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, Tathāgata!"
"You should now have Mañjuśrī go and seek the bowl.
The Buddha then said to Mañjuśrī, "Go and seek the bowl; come back when you have found it."

Mañjuśrī immediately became silent; having received the instruction, he reflected within himself, yet he did not rise from his seat, nor leave the Buddha, nor depart from the assembly, and was thus able to bring forth the bowl.

At that moment, his samādhi entered everywhere without exception; he then pointed to the ground with his hand amidst the assembly, and as his hand descended, every Buddha-field it passed through had all the Buddhas receive his feet. Throughout the lower regions, there was no one who did not hear the voice proclaiming:
"Śākyamuni Buddha sends his greetings."

From each hair-pore of his arms, hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light were emitted; from each ray of light, there appeared hundreds of thousands of millions of lotuses; upon each lotus sat a bodhisattva, and each of those bodhisattvas offered praise to Śākyamuni Buddha.

All the buddha-fields they passed through shook in six ways; in those fields, banners and streamers were all raised in solemn adornment. Throughout their entire journey, Mañjuśrī was seen with his right hand receiving the feet of all the Buddhas, and everyone said, "This is the inquiry sent by Śākyamuni Buddha."

Passing through lands as numerous as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers, he arrived at the land called Mingkaipì (Luminous Opening), reaching the presence of the Buddha Tāpilaraya. He prostrated before him and inquired after the health of Śākyamuni Buddha on his behalf.

On each hair of his arms, there were hundreds of millions of rays of light and hundreds of millions of lotus flowers; upon each lotus flower sat a bodhisattva, all of whom extolled the merits of Śākyamuni Buddha.
The radiance of that bodhisattva and the radiance of that Buddha did not intermingle; each saw, by their own light, an attendant beside the Buddha King of Radiance.
There was a noble bodhisattva named Light Honored One (*Prabhāpūjita*) who asked his Buddha, "Whose arms are so exceedingly beautiful?"
The radiance of its fur is that which the Bodhisattva Padma praises as the merits of that Buddha.
That Buddha said:
“Above, passing through lands as numerous as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers, there is a world-system named Sahā; the Buddha there is named Śākyamuni, and he currently resides before us.”

There is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, whose monastic community is inconceivable and whose wisdom is all-pervading; he remains continuously before that Buddha, and for the sake of his almsbowl, he extended his hand until it reached this place.
Those bodhisattvas all had this thought and addressed their Buddha, saying:
"Just as a thirsty person desires to drink, we wish to behold Śākyamuni Buddha, Mañjuśrī, and their buddha-field."

That Buddha immediately emitted a radiance from the mark between his two eyebrows, which shone through and beyond lands as numerous as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers, until even the Sahā world-system was entirely opened up; all those who beheld that radiance attained peace and security.
His body was like that of a Cakravartin king; among the ordinary bhikṣus there were those who had attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Those who surpassed the three paths all possessed the eight stages of *dhyāna* (the *aṣṭavimokṣa*), and at that time they attained Arhatship.
Those bodhisattvas whose bodies receive this radiance all attain the *sūryaprabhā-samādhi*.
All the bodhisattvas from the buddha-field of the Buddha Tathāgata Candrasūryapradīpa see this world and all its śrāvakas and bodhisattvas from that very place.
Seeing this world-system in such a state, he shed tears and said:
"If clear lapis lazuli and mani jewels were to fall into this foul mud, it would truly be a pity."
"Why is this? It is truly lamentable that the bodhisattvas of the Sahā world-system have been born in that place.
The Buddha Dīpaṃkara said to the Bodhisattva Pāyāsi:
"You do not understand this; do not speak of it. Why is that?

Though I have practiced meditation in my own buddha-field for a thousand kalpas, it does not equal the merit of a person in that Buddha-field who practices loving-kindness from sunrise until mealtime; the latter's merit exceeds the former many times over."
"Even though that bodhisattva possesses the recollection of past lives, if he practices the Dharma for even as long as a finger-snap, his transgressions will be completely exhausted.
Thereupon, the bodhisattvas there all asked the Buddha,
"From where does this radiance come?"
"Now all bodies are at peace.
The Buddha then said:
"Below this world, past as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in seventy-two Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Ukāśa."
"Who is this Buddha?
His name is Dīpaṃkara; he emits the radiance from the mark between his two eyebrows.
The Bodhisattvas all addressed the Buddha:
“I wish to hear and to see the world-system of Ukhasa and the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.

At that moment, Śākyamuni emitted a radiance from beneath his feet, which illuminated the regions below, passing through world-systems as numerous as the sands of seventy-two Ganges Rivers; the world-system of Ukhasa and the Buddha Dīpaṃkara were all fully revealed.
The bodhisattvas of that land see that light enter their bodies, whereby they all attain the *mabhidi* samādhi—*mabhidi* being the Indic term for which the Han translation is "Sumeru-light."
In this world, the bodhisattvas see all those Buddhas and their lands; it is just as those dwelling upon the earth cannot fail to see the sun, moon, and stars.
Just as those below see this world, so too do those in this world see the *Tāpīlaya-ughasa* buddha-field below.
Mañjuśrī took the bowl with his right hand and, together with countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of bodhisattvas, ascended upward.
As they passed through the various buddha-fields, the lotus flowers that had emanated from each pore of light gradually faded away, until the bowl remained entirely in his hand.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and presented the bowl to him; the Buddha then accepted it.
All the bodhisattvas who had ascended from below likewise paid their respects, each individually expressing gratitude to Śākyamuni Buddha by citing his name.
The Tathāgata immediately commanded each of them to take their seats;
they all followed the instruction and sat down one by one.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"What you have asked just now was prompted by the inquiry of Mañjuśrī; therefore, I shall now explain it for you.
In the past, incalculable, immeasurable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Unconquerable Valor, and his buddha-field was called Impermanence."
At that time, eighty-four thousand śrāvakas and twelve thousand bodhisattvas were all assembled together; for those of the three vehicles, the Buddha preached the Dharma accordingly.
The Buddha said:
"At that time, the Tathāgata, whose valor was invincible, became a Buddha in the fivefold evil age.

There was a bhikṣu named Prajñārāja, who was erudite in the sūtras and dharmas. Carrying his alms bowl, he entered the city of Vaidiśa to wander for alms and obtained food of a hundred flavors and various kinds of delicacies."
At that time, there was the son of an elder named Vimalarāja, who was being held by his nursemaid and was standing outside the city gate.
From afar, the boy saw a bhikṣu learned in the sūtras; wishing to descend from his nurse’s arms, he did so and approached him seeking food. The bhikṣu then gave him honey-cakes.

The child ate it and, finding its flavor sweet and delicious, followed the bhikṣu without looking back at his nurse. He followed him all the way to where the Buddha Śūra-maṅgala was, prostrated before the Buddha, and sat to one side.
If the bhikṣu Nārāyaṇa takes the food he has received in his alms bowl and gives it to this boy, instructing him to offer it to that Buddha, the boy will accept it and present it to the Tathāgata.
When that Buddha accepted the food, his bowl became full, yet the food in the bowl held by the boy continued as before.
Furthermore, with this same food, he satisfied eighty-four thousand bhikṣus and twelve thousand bodhisattvas, each being fully satiated, while the food held by the boy continued to remain as it was.

The Buddha, through his majestic spiritual power, caused the boy to rejoice; by virtue of his original merit, he immediately attained complete faith. He then stepped forward and stood before him, extolling the Buddha and offering the food held in his bowl as an alms-offering.

Because it was timely and sufficient, that which was held did not diminish; the food continued to be present for all the bhikṣus and bodhisattvas, whereby it was known that even though the Honored Buddha had partaken, it was not exhausted but increased once more.
"The merit of those who make offerings to the Buddha is weighty and shall increase.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"This boy offered a single bowl of food; even after seven days, that food did not diminish, remaining full as it was before."

That Buddha, Aparājita, instructed his son to take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; he conferred upon him the five precepts, taught him to repent of his transgressions, and exhorted him to cultivate merit.
He then gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The child’s parents searched everywhere for their son without exception, even reaching the presence of the *tathāgata*, where they stood before the Buddha and paid him homage.
When the son saw his parents, he went before them, paid homage, and spoke these words of praise:
"I have now entered the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas; for the sake of all beings, I vow to resolve my mind once again."
"Why is this? Because a Buddha is difficult to encounter.
He then said to his parents:
"Beholding the marks and secondary characteristics of the Buddha, his wisdom is all-pervasive, and his Way brings deliverance.
I vow that my body shall be permitted to become a śramaṇa."
"Why is this? Because it is difficult to meet with a Tathāgata.
His parents then said:
"Excellent, excellent!
Enjoy yourself according to your desires.
Whatever you seek shall be fulfilled exactly as you wish."
"We, too, shall resolve our minds to follow you in the Dharma; we now relinquish all our homes and dwellings, and likewise emulate you by becoming śramaṇas."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"Regarding what this boy has said, his parents and five hundred others have all resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and they shall all become śramaṇas under the Buddha Aparājitadhvaja."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Regarding those whom you have doubted: the bhikṣu Nārāyaṇa was none other than Mañjuśrī; at that time, the noble son Vimalakīrti was my very self."

Mañjuśrī gave me this food, and by performing this meritorious deed, he caused me to resolve my mind [upon enlightenment]; he is thus the original teacher who inspired my initial aspiration for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“If you wish to know that the ten powers of this present Buddha and the four grounds of self-confidence, whose wisdom is inconceivable, are all set in motion by Mañjuśrī.”
"Why is this? Because the mind is the root.
The Buddha spoke again to Śāriputra:
"Just as my own body and those of the Buddhas in incalculable, asankhyeya world-systems are all impelled by Mañjuśrī, and are all named Śākyamuni Buddha."
In this number of Buddhas, there was again one named Ti-shi-fei Buddha, another named Shi Buddha, another named Ti-ho-jie Buddha, and another named Wei-wei Buddha.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:

“To speak exhaustively of the names of all these Buddhas would take from kalpa to kalpa without reaching their end; yet all are set in motion by Mañjuśrī. Among those who are currently turning the wheel of Dharma, some have entered parinirvāṇa, some are practicing the bodhisattva path, some are in the Tuṣita Heaven, some are in their mothers’ wombs, some have been born, some have left home to seek Buddhahood, some are sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, and some have attained Buddhahood—yet even these remain inexhaustible.”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Mañjuśrī is the father and mother of bodhisattvas; he is their kalyāṇamitra.
Regarding what you have just asked, for what reason do you set aside the Tathāgata?"
"The attainment I have achieved is entirely due to the grace of Mañjuśrī;
it is because of this grace that these two hundred sons of gods immediately thought to themselves:
'Only those who study all dharmas can achieve accomplishment, and we are capable of doing so.'"
Why is this? Now, this Śākyamuni Buddha attained the state of Buddhahood through the resolve first inspired by Mañjuśrī; why, then, should we be indolent?
"Because of this reflection, his mind becomes firm, and he attains complete faith in the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Mañjuśrī, by means of a hand-transformation, obtained a bowl; there was nothing it did not move. This is called the fundamental training."
From this land down to the lower regions, there were incalculable numbers of people who all resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

All the Buddhas currently residing in the ten directions used precious jeweled canopies as offerings to the Dharma; these canopies completely covered the trichiliocosm, and from within them, one could hear their voices entirely, just as Śākyamuni Buddha spoke—everything was moved by Mañjuśrī.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“If any man or woman wishes to enter parinirvāṇa swiftly, they should resolve their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

Why is this? There are those who, fearing birth and death, are unable to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, but instead seek to become *śrāvakas* and attain the state of an *arhat* to enter *parinirvāṇa* prematurely.
As for those who speak such words, I continue to see them remaining within the cycle of birth and death.
There are bodhisattvas who are diligent and have already attained Buddhahood. Why is this so?
In the past, incalculable, immeasurable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Sarvābhibhū; his lifespan was ten thousand years, and he had ten billion disciples.
There was a venerable bhikṣu named Ajita, whose wisdom was most sublime.
Later, there was a venerable bhikṣu named Mahāpraṇidhānaprāpta, whose supernormal powers were likewise most sublime.
At that time, the Tathāgata adjusted his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the kingdom of Nityayaśas together with the bhikṣus to beg for food.

The venerable bhikṣu who was fully endowed with wisdom stood to the right of the Buddha; the bhikṣu possessed of supernormal powers stood to the left of the Buddha; and there was a venerable bhikṣu named Kaukṛtyajñāna, who followed behind the Buddha to attend upon him.

Eight thousand bodhisattvas led the way in front; among them were some who appeared like Śakra, some dressed like devaputras, some like devas, and some like the four heavenly kings, all of whom had people prepare the road for the sake of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra: "At that time,
as the Buddha was passing through the marketplace on the road leading into that city,
there were three sons of noble families, each still quite young, who were sitting together playing, their garments and ornaments most exquisitely beautiful."
One of the boys saw from afar that the Buddha was approaching, along with the bhikṣus and bodhisattvas, their radiance most majestic and sublime.

The younger boy pointed him out from a distance with his hand to the two other boys, saying, "Look! The Tathāgata is coming; it is truly wondrous how great is this radiance and its accompanying retinue."
The two sons then said,
"We have seen it.
One of them spoke further:
"This one is the most supreme among all things and has no equal; we should make offerings to him. Why is this?
Because his merit is immeasurable."
The two sons replied, "There are no flowers or incense;
with what then shall we make our offering?
One of the sons then took off the white pearl he was wearing on his body, placed it in his hand, and said to the other two sons:
"This is indeed fit to be offered to the Buddha, the Knower.
Having seen the Tathāgata, they should not harbor greed.

Then the two boys, imitating their understanding, took the white pearls from their heads and placed them in his hands; they each uttered a sigh of praise and proceeded toward the Buddha’s dwelling as if crossing over water.
Why is this? Because their minds are pure and they abide in equanimity.
Then, one boy asked the other two boys:
"What do you seek with these merits?
One of the sons replied,
"I wish to become like the Venerable Bhikṣu on the Buddha’s right."
One of the sons said,
"I wish to be like the bhikṣu with supernormal powers on the left side.
After each of these two sons had made their respective vows, they together questioned another son:
"What is your wish?
he asked. He replied:
"I desire to be like the Buddha, with a radiance beyond compare, walking alone like a lion, and always having a multitude following me."
When the boy spoke these words, eight thousand devaputras in the void all exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!
Just as you have said, all those in the heavens and on earth shall receive your grace."
These three boys brought him together before the Buddha.
The Tathāgata called to his attendant Śāriputra:
"Do you see these three boys who have come bringing white pearls?"
When the child walking in the center proceeds with a joyful mind and focused diligence, at the moment he lifts one foot, his offenses for a hundred kalpas are eliminated.
For every step he takes, he shall subsequently become a Cakravartin King a hundred times over.

In this same number, there shall again be further explanations as well; the Brahmā heavens are likewise equal in this regard, and within the merit of a single step taken, one perceives a hundred Buddhas.
As soon as he had finished speaking, the three boys arrived; they came forward, paid homage to the Tathāgata, and each scattered white pearls over the Buddha.
The two sons who had resolved their minds toward the stage of Śrāvaka, the pearls they scattered each rose up above the Buddha’s shoulders;

the one son who had resolved his mind toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi scattered white pearls upon the Buddha’s head, which transformed in mid-air into a jeweled canopy of interlaced pearls, perfectly symmetrical on all four sides, within which was a throne where the Tathāgata sat.
That Buddha then smiled.
Śāriputra asked the Buddha,
"The Tathāgata’s smile must surely have a specific meaning."
"I wish to hear your explanation.
The Buddha said,
"Did you see the two children resolve their intent toward the stage of Śrāvaka?"
Why is this? It is because they all fear the terrors of birth and death; for this reason, they do not resolve to attain the mind of a bodhisattva. Why is this?
"Because he wishes to enter parinirvāṇa quickly.
His attendant asked,
"What shall become of that other son?"
The Buddha spoke again, saying:

"This middle son shall later attain Buddhahood for himself; these two sons shall become his śrāvakas—one of them will possess wisdom that is most preeminent, and the other will likewise possess supernormal powers."
Śākyamuni Buddha asked Śāriputra:
"Do you know who this child in the center is?
Śāriputra replied:
"Not so," the Buddha said.
"It was I myself."
"Do you know the child on the right side?
Śāriputra replied, "I do not."
"The child at that time was Śāriputra;
the child on his left side was Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Because you were originally afraid of birth and death, you did not resolve to attain the Bodhisattva mind, desiring instead to enter parinirvāṇa quickly.
Observe that one of your sons has resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; now I myself have attained Buddhahood."
"Just as you have not departed from my Dharma, yet by becoming śrāvakas you have attained liberation.
The Buddha spoke again to Śāriputra:
"Those who wish to enter parinirvāṇa quickly should resolve their minds to seek Buddhahood just as I have."
That which was previously described as being most swift is none other than *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge). Why is this? Because it is free from all obstructions;

because it is upheld by the Honored One; because it is inexhaustible; because it is the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; because nothing can equal or surpass it; because it maintains what is excellent; and because it transcends all *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
"Those who wish to practice it shall likewise attain the mind of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) in this very same way.
When this "Chapter on the Mahāyāna" was preached, ten thousand people all resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Each of those venerable bhikṣus—Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Ānanda, Śāṇavāsin, Mahākāśyapa, Kapphiṇa, Revata, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Subhūti—bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and all praised him, saying:
“If any man or woman desires to seek the Way, they should resolve upon the noble intention.”

Why is this? Although the Buddha has taught us the Dharma in hundreds of thousands of ways, we are unable to give rise once more to the bodhicitta; instead, we all regret our pursuit of arhatship. It would be better for us to have previously committed the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), for even those sins can still be liberated from, and one may resolve to attain the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Now, this is of no benefit whatsoever.
Why is that? It is solely because it burns away the seeds of Buddhahood.
Those who possess such vessels are incapable of the bodhisattva mind.
Why is this? It is because they are like a dead person, who is of no benefit to the living.
Now that we have escaped, it will be of no benefit to those above or below in heaven or on earth.
Whether they be two-footed or four-footed, all beings depend upon the earth to live.
"Whoever gives rise to the mind for Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, both devas and humans shall all receive their grace.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru, riding in a carriage drawn by four horses and accompanied by his ministers, went out to the place where the Buddha was. He approached, prostrated himself in salutation, and stood before him, addressing the Buddha:
"By what causes and conditions do all people commit offenses?"
The Buddha said to Ajātaśatru:
"One who dwells in the notions of 'self' and 'person' commits offenses; because one craves the body, there is the employment of the body, and for this reason, one does not depart from within it."
King Ajātaśatru asked again:
“In what does the root of that which assists craving reside?
The Buddha said:
"Lack of wisdom is it.
He then asked again:
"What is the faculty of lack of wisdom?"
The Buddha said:
"Because what is done differs from what is remembered, it is therefore called a faculty (indriya).
He asked again:
"What is it that differs from mindfulness?
The Buddha said:
"That which is fundamentally different from what is produced—this is what is meant."
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'originally different'?
The Buddha said:
"Just as that which is conjured by illusion has no real existence, so too are they different.
He asked again:
"Who is it that conjures?"
The Buddha said:
"Because there is no creator, it is an emanation.
He asked again:
"If there is nothing produced and nothing existing, how can one calculate it?
The Buddha said,
"Because there is no production and nothing exists, it cannot be calculated."
He asked again:
"From what causes and conditions does your doubt arise?
The Buddha said:
“Because there is nothing upon which to rely.
“What is meant by ‘having nothing upon which to rely’?
The Buddha said:
"To hear what has been taught and yet harbor doubts about it is called 'not relying [on the teaching].
He asked again: 'What is the Way?'"
"What constitutes faith?
The Buddha said,
"To be liberated from lust, anger, and delusion— this is the Way."
"What is this faith?
The Buddha said,
"Not grasping at the root of any phenomena, and the mind remaining undifferentiated— this is why it is called faith."
King Ajātaśatru then said:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is just as the Tathāgata has taught."
Why is it that all people do not believe me?
It is because I acted on my own initiative.

Now, following the words of wicked men, I have commanded my subordinates to kill their own fathers—driven by greed for the state, greed for wealth and treasures, greed for the benefits of governing the people, and greed for honor and nobility.

Now my ministers have humiliated me and harmed their own father; greedy for life and filled with doubt, they cannot resolve it themselves. Whether drinking or eating, whether in play and pleasure, whether in the main hall attending to state affairs, whether in the inner palace amidst the five desires, or whether alone or in a crowd, they do not forget it day or night. Consequently, they cannot digest their food, they find no sleep, and their countenances lack any trace of serenity.
At that time, his heart was constantly filled with dread, knowing he would not escape the hells.
He then spoke again:

“If one who is blind receives eyes through the Buddha, if one who is drowning in water relies on the Buddha to be delivered, if those who have suffering find peace through the Buddha, if those who are terrified receive protection from the Buddha, if those who are impoverished can obtain precious jewels through the Buddha, and if those who have lost their way can be shown the path by him—”

The Buddha, through his great compassion, does not regard this as toil or hardship; he maintains an impartial mind toward all, acting with steadfastness and kindness, and constantly enduring both suffering and joy without abandoning any person.
Now my body is filled with fear and trembling; may the Buddha alone grant his protection, so that those in peril may find peace.
Since there is no one capable of saving this body, I pray only for deliverance. Having nowhere else to turn, I pray that you will accept my taking refuge in your life.
It is as if one who lacks eyesight were to gain the ability to see, or as if a person wishing to walk with crippled legs were to gain the power to go;
now that we are about to enter the Avīci hell and even the great Niraya hells, I pray that we may not enter them.

I pray that the Tathāgata will now explain for me and resolve my doubts, so that my mind may attain liberation and remain free from further uncertainty until death, and so that my grave offenses may be lightened.

The Buddha thought to himself: "King Ajātaśatru’s discourse is profoundly deep and subtle; this ailment cannot be cured by anyone else, but only the Buddha and Mañjuśrī possess the power to respond to it."
Śāriputra, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, said to Ajātaśatru:

"If you wish to resolve your doubts, prepare food tomorrow morning and invite Mañjuśrī and his retinue to your palace to receive it. All your officials and subordinates shall thereby obtain merit, and all the people of Rājagṛha may likewise take this meritorious deed as their foundation."
King Ajātaśatru then addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"I pray that you will show me great kindness by deigning to visit my palace for a meal tomorrow morning.
To this, Mañjuśrī replied:
"It is sufficient to have made offerings with your feet.
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
"The Buddha-dharma does not consist of food or clothing."
Ajātaśatru then asked:
"How should one give it?
To which he replied:

"If one enters deeply into the subtle, and its matters are examined with such certainty that there is no defilement and no attachment, no doubt and no difficulty, no fear and no single dread—such a person is said to have attained compassion."
Mañjuśrī spoke again to Ajātaśatru:
"To contemplate all dharmas without contemplating existence and without contemplating non-existence—this is what constitutes attaining compassion."
One should not dwell on thoughts of the past, nor should one dwell on thoughts of the future, nor should one dwell on thoughts of the present; by acting in this way, one attains compassion.
"You should not think of anything that can be seen, nor should you truly act as such; thus you shall receive my compassion.
King Ajātaśatru spoke again to Mañjuśrī:
"As you have said, all things contained within the Dharma are without exception; yet, for the sake of this body alone, may you show compassion and accept my request."
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
"Cease for a moment.
That which is the Way is not for the sake of drinking or eating."
If a king does not conceive of "I," "mine," "self," "life-span," or "person," and because he does not conceive these things, he attains compassion.

If his mind holds nothing and has no object of focus—neither the four great elements nor the five aggregates, neither the six sense-decays nor the maintenance of the three realms; neither regarding merit nor conceiving of the absence of merit; neither regarding the mundane nor the supramundane, neither regarding transgression nor non-transgression; neither regarding the remainder nor the remainderless, neither regarding liberation nor non-liberation, neither regarding birth-and-death nor nirvana—one who acts in this way attains compassion.
King Ajātaśatru spoke again to Mañjuśrī:
“Hearing such a Dharma as this, I am all the more filled with joy; for this reason, I wish to invite you, so that by means of this, I may attain peace and security.”
Mañjuśrī replied:
"You hope for an object of focus in order to attain peace; therefore, if there is no such focus, there is no peace. Why is this so? Because..."

Because that dharma has no object of perception and no stability, one does not dwell upon it nor become conceited; being entirely without mental engagement, one is therefore peaceful by virtue of this very condition.
Within this there is no ill will, and later there shall be no calamities or transformations.
That which undergoes calamities and transformations later is not peaceful; that which remains without change from beginning to end is what constitutes peace.
Ajātaśatru asked again:
"What Dharma do you teach such that there is no distinction to be found, yet peace is attained?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"If emptiness has no agent, there is no one capable of acting; there is no perception, no aspiration, no activity, and furthermore, no actor."
If one has thoughts that there is something to be done or nothing to be done, for this reason it is different.
Furthermore, one does not seek the absence of an object of perception; body, speech, and mind constitute "action."
Why is this? Because there is no perception of birth and death.
Therefore, regarding all phenomena, if they appear to have an object of perception, one should know that they are entirely without an object of perception.
Ajātaśatru asked again:
"What is meant by 'birth-and-death and the absence of birth-and-death'? He replied:
One does not dwell on the past as it has ended, nor does one dwell on the future as it has not yet arrived, nor does one dwell on the present as being impermanent.
Regarding all phenomena, one does not dwell on anything being increased or decreased; where there is no such agent, there is neither birth-and-death nor the cessation of birth-and-death.
Ajātaśatru asked again:
"How should one who has not yet attained liberation unite with the Way?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Do you know whether the brightness of the sun merges with darkness?
Ajātaśatru replied,
"They do not merge."
"Why is this? When the sun rises, all darkness and obscurity are extinguished. Mañjuśrī said:
"Does Your Majesty know where the darkness goes?
He replied, "I do not see a place where it can abide; in what location could it dwell?"

Mañjuśrī said: "When so-called 'knowledge of the path' (mārgajñatā) arises, it is like the rising of the sun, whereby one cannot know where the various darknesses reside; likewise, at such a time, one does not know where those who have not yet been liberated reside."
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
“The Path is equal to those who have not yet been liberated, and those who have not yet been liberated are equal to the Path. Why is this?
Because both are empty, and because that which is not yet liberated is equal to the Path.
All dharmas are equal; for one who knows this, that which is not yet liberated becomes the Path. Why is this?
"To seek that which is not liberated and not know its location—therefore it is called the Way (mārga).
To seek the location of non-liberation and find it invisible—that is the Way.
Ajātaśatru asked again:
“What is it that is not liberated yet constitutes the Way?
Mañjuśrī replied, “To be within non-liberation is the Way; to not act in this manner is the Way.”
Ajātaśatru asked again:
"How should that Way be studied?
He then replied:
"Learning all dharmas as they are.
Ajātaśatru asked again,
"In learning all dharmas, is there any fixed location?"
Mañjuśrī said, “One who trains in this manner cannot attain it.
Ajātaśatru asked again:
"Will those who study this reach nirvāṇa?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Is there any dharma that comes from nirvāṇa, such that one could say, 'I have come from nirvāṇa'?"
Ajātaśatru then said,
“There is neither one who goes, nor one who comes.
Mañjuśrī said to Ajātaśatru:
"Because one who studies the Way knows that it has no location, therefore it is called the 'Way'.
Ajātaśatru asked again:
"In what state should one abide while practicing this study of the Way?"
He replied, “To have no abiding place is what it means to study the Way.
Ajātaśatru asked again:
“Does one who studies the Way not abide in pure precepts, samādhi, and wisdom?
He replied: “One who follows the Way does not take precepts as a causal object, does not seek samādhi, and does not become arrogant regarding their abiding in wisdom.”
Mañjuśrī said to Ajātaśatru:
"If one relies on the precepts, seeks samādhi, yet is arrogant regarding wisdom—would such a person have a place of abiding?"
Ajātaśatru said, "No. Mañjuśrī said:
"Therefore, one should abide nowhere, just as the Way does.
Ajātaśatru asked again:
"If there are men or women, how should they advance toward the Way?"

Mañjuśrī said: "Those who wish to study the Way do not perceive dharmas as being permanent or impermanent; they do not perceive dharmas as being liberated or unliberated; nor do they perceive dharmas as being peaceful or suffering; nor do they perceive dharmas as being 'self' or 'belonging to all persons'; nor do they perceive dharmas as being within saṃsāra or reaching nirvāṇa. One who studies the Way in this manner is foremost."
King Ajātaśatru then said:
"Excellent, excellent!
It is just as Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva has spoken."
I only pray that you will accept this invitation. Why is this?
It is because of doubt.
"I have reflected deeply upon this: while all dharmas are without self, without a person, without a life-principle, and without a soul, I still harbor doubts.

Mañjuśrī said, "That which is non-existent cannot be made to exist. Because it is non-existent, there is neither liberation nor anything to be liberated from. As for those who speak of a 'self' and claim there is liberation, since no such self exists, there is neither liberation nor anything to be liberated from."
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are completely liberated.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"Because he has accepted King Ajātaśatru’s invitation for the sake of countless people.
Mañjuśrī then said, "I accept only the teaching of the Tathāgata."
"Why is this? Because it does not contradict the teaching.
Ajātaśatru then leaped for joy and, rising from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, the bhikṣus, and Mañjuśrī, and departed.
King Ajātaśatru, while walking, asked Śāriputra,
"How many are there among those such as Mañjuśrī?
Śāriputra replied:
"Let all five hundred people eat in the palace.
He then returned to the city from the road and immediately commanded the chief steward to prepare food of a hundred flavors.
