On that very day, he adorned the palace hall, setting up banners, streamers, curtains, canopies, and flowered awnings; he spread flowers upon the ground and perfumed it all with famous incense.
Five hundred high couches were prepared, all spread with famous pearls and *wanli* gems of various colors; the entire palace was thoroughly adorned and perfumed with flowers and incense.

An imperial decree was issued to sweep clean all city walls, streets, markets, and villages, and to follow him with exquisite incense. Along the roadsides, canopies, curtains, banners, and streamers were set up and cleared away; at the gates of every village, double-knotted flowers were displayed, and the people were ordered to welcome and make offerings to him along the road on the following morning.
Then, during the first watch of the night, Mañjuśrī thought to himself:

"If I go with only a few others to this invitation, there will be no other great stirrings; it would be better to invite the bodhisattvas from other buddha-fields to that place, have them attend the invitation, and furthermore, let them all hear the Dharma being preached."

While he was thinking this, in the time it takes to extend one’s arm, he vanished from that place and arrived in the east, passing through eighty-two thousand Buddha-fields. That field is named Constant Renown; the Buddha there is named Pure Pinnacle, who currently resides there. There are only bodhisattvas and no other paths, and in that buddha-field, the irreversible wheel of Dharma is constantly turned.

All the trees in that land are made entirely of various jewels; their leaves, flowers, and fruits are of countless colors. When a breeze arises and blows through those trees, one hears only the voice of the Buddha, the voice of the Dharma, and the voice of the *avaivartika* Saṃgha.
Because they constantly hear the sound of the Triple Gem there, that buddha-field is named Śatadru-guḍa.
Mañjuśrī was already present in that place; he paid homage to the Buddha and addressed the Tathāgata, saying:
"For my sake, I pray that you cause all the bodhisattvas to go to the Sahā world-system and attend the meal at the place of Ajātaśatru."
The Buddha then said to him,
"If you wish to go, you may depart.
*The Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru*, Volume One.
In the *Buddhabhāṣita-ajātashatru-rāja-sūtra*, Scroll II,
translated by the Yuezhi Tripiṭaka Master Zhi Loujiachen of the Later Han Dynasty,
at that moment twenty-two thousand bodhisattvas raised their voices in unison: "We wish to [be with] Mañjuśrī..."
“Mañjuśrī, let us go together.
Immediately, as many bodhisattvas as there were number, they set out with Mañjuśrī and suddenly arrived at the place where the Sahā world-system was located and sat down.
The place where they stayed was within the hall; that it could accommodate them all was due to the majestic spiritual power of the Bodhisattva.
Once they had all taken their seats, Mañjuśrī expounded the Dharma for them, and the name of that Dharma was *dhāraṇī*.
Mañjuśrī said to the bodhisattvas: "Do you know what dharma is called *dhāraṇī*? It is because it understands all dharmas; because its intention is free from expectation;

because its actions are without distinction; because its mindfulness is sufficient for the occasion; because its knowledge accords with wisdom; because it fully knows the root of all those dharmas; because its speech accords with truth; because it guards itself so as not to fall away; because it employs itself to progress upward; and because it enters entirely into the practice of all dharmas."
Dhāraṇī is the source of the Way; it is the source of not severing the lineage of the Buddha, the source of upholding the Dharma, and the source of the Saṃgha’s total retention.
It is without fail regarding all dharmas; whatever a person asks, one is immediately able to know and provide an answer.
He beholds the multitude and does not withdraw. Why is this?
Because he is free from fear.
Desiring to transform and guide the various devas, he teaches them all according to their respective inclinations, causing each to attain understanding.

Furthermore, regarding nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as Śakra and Brahmā, down to all insects, beasts, and birds—he knows the thoughts of each and, according to their desires, transforms and guides them all so that they may find their proper place.
Fully understanding both that which possesses merit and that which lacks it, they know the conduct and abiding of all people; their minds are like the earth.

They do not dwell upon the eight worldly concerns, but accord with whatever meritorious deeds are performed. Without departing from the Way and its teachings, they illuminate others, causing all to receive their grace according to their inclinations.

The precepts they practice encompass all things; their wisdom penetrates everywhere without exception; they are honored by all, yet do not regard this as toil or hardship, for their minds remain without variation.
Regarding that Dharma, one knows it as the very basis of what has been taught and transformed.
Receiving its instruction, one constantly bestows it through the Dharma without ever becoming weary; regarding the Dharma one preaches, one does not hope for any reward in return.
Furthermore, they do not sever the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva. Why is this?
Because through diligence, they cultivate and bring those roots to maturity.
One does not become weary or satisfied with what one gives, because of the sake of sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
One does not become weary or satisfied with the precepts. Why is this?
Because he respects all people, he practices patience without ever being satisfied; thus, he attains the body of a Buddha.
Because he applies diligence without ever being satisfied, he brings together all merits.
One does not become weary or satisfied with meditative concentration because one harbors no expectations;
likewise, one is never weary or satisfied with wisdom. Why is this so?
Because there is nothing that is not brought to mind;
taking the Dharma as one’s salary and relying upon it for sustenance, one has no involvement in anything else.
One who is thus is therefore called a *dhāraṇī*.
Dhāraṇī means that it universally upholds all dharmas.
How does it uphold them?
Because it is empty, signless, wishless, desireless, unattached, and without views.
By means of this upholding, there is nothing produced and nothing created.
To act as this upholder of the Dharma is to neither come nor go, neither abide nor be distracted, neither proceed nor perish; it is to have nothing upheld and nothing grasped.

Regarding liberation, one does not conceive of it as liberation; there is no dwelling, nor should there be any dwelling. There is no "mine" and no self, no life-span and no person. There is neither grasping nor relinquishing, neither reality nor unreality. There is nothing heard and nothing seen; like space, it cannot be described or measured. There is nothing touched and nothing perceived. Because it sustains all dharmas, it is called *dhāraṇī*.

Furthermore, there is *dhāraṇī*, which maintains all dharmas as being like illusions, comparable to dreams or mirages, comparable to clusters of foam on water or bubbles, and comparable to magical transformations; because it maintains all dharmas in this way, it is called *dhāraṇī*.

Furthermore, there is a *dhāraṇī* which upholds all phenomena through impermanence. If one perceives that they are selfless and quiescent, one is entirely liberated from the root of all phenomena therein. One does not contend with phenomena, nor does one fall [into extremes], nor is there any expectation. Because it upholds all phenomena in this way, it is called *dhāraṇī*.
Just as the earth sustains everything without exception and does not consider this a laborious task, so too the Bodhisattva who has attained *dhāraṇī* serves as the foundation for all;

throughout incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he is able to gather together all the merits he has performed to give rise to omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). His mind sustains nothing that it cannot hold, yet he neither releases nor finds it troublesome.
Why is this so? It is because the earth serves as the foundation and support for all things.
Likewise, a bodhisattva who has attained dharani benefits all beings, just as trees and the myriad things grow depending upon the earth.
When a bodhisattva has attained dharani, all dharmas of merit arise within them.
It is like the earth: it neither moves nor shakes; it has no preference and harbors no aversion.
Just as the earth receives all rain without ever becoming weary or exhausted,

so too the bodhisattva who has attained dharani is never satiated by the teachings questioned by all buddhas, bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, nor does he ever grow weary of preaching the Dharma for the sake of all beings.
It is like the earth, which contains the seeds of all fruits so that they may emerge at their proper time.

A bodhisattva who has attained *dhāraṇī* likewise contains the seeds of all meritorious dharmas; they do not miss their timing, but rather, as the time comes, they become fully endowed with all dharmas, and thus sit beneath the Bodhi tree without departing from omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
Because a bodhisattva who has attained dhāraṇī is as courageous as a general, whom no one among the troops can fail to submit to;
because a bodhisattva who has reached the attainment of dhāraṇī sits beneath the Bodhi tree and subdues all Māras, it is therefore called "dhāraṇī."
Furthermore, there is a *dhāraṇī* which holds nothing among all phenomena.

Why is this? Because it is neither permanent nor impermanent; it is neither pleasure nor pain; it is neither having a body nor not having a body; it is neither a person nor permanence. Thus, all phenomena are without anything to be held.
Why is this? Because there are no two minds.
Just as the earth does not support space, so too, within the *dhāraṇī*, all phenomena have nothing that is supported.
Just as space does not possess anything that can be possessed, so too the dhāraṇī possesses nothing among all phenomena.
Just as water does not retain any impurities or turbidity, so too the dhāraṇī possesses nothing among all phenomena.
It is like reaching a destination that has no fixed location;

because the *dhāraṇī* has nothing to be grasped, it is inexhaustible and without end, and because it cannot be measured, there is nowhere it does not enter. Because there is nowhere it does not enter, it is the realm of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dhātu*).
"Dhāraṇī is equal to emptiness.
When he spoke these words on dhāraṇī, five hundred bodhisattvas all attained the dharma of dhāraṇī.
During the second watch of the night, Mañjuśrī taught the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.

"There is no phenomenon that does not proceed from this: whether it be dharmas of merit or dharmas without merit, whether mundane or supramundane, whether with fault or without fault, whether with remainder or without remainder, whether liberated or unliberated—all are entirely contained within this treasury."
Why is this? It is because all dharmas are employed and there is nothing that is not attained.

It is, for example, as if a trichiliocosm world-system—containing ten billion lands, ten billion suns and moons, ten billion Mount Sumerus, and ten billion great oceans—were entirely contained within that single trichiliocosm.
Neither mundane dharmas nor supramundane dharmas fail to enter into it.
The dharmas of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas all enter into it.
Why is this? Because it universally upholds all practices—upholding those of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, and the bodhisattvas.
Just as when the roots of a tree are firmly established, its trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will all flourish and become excellent.
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka upholds everything and accomplishes everything; it sustains all dharmas of merit and fully maintains the mind of sarvajñatā (omniscience).
As for this Bodhisattva-piṭaka, it is like a vessel called "receptacle," which cannot be numbered.

It is like the ocean, which receives and holds all waters and sustains precious treasures; it encompasses dragons, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, serving as their dwelling place for all.

The causes and conditions for that treasury are likewise incalculable; it receives innumerable precepts, and within it, the samādhis and wisdom perceive such that there is no vessel that does not receive or see. Therefore, it is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
It is like the great ocean: those who go there to dwell do not drink other waters. Why is this?
It is entirely because of the ocean.
Those who are within this treasury all rely on this Dharma and do not belong to the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika). Why is this?
Because they have fully received the flavor of the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) Dharma; therefore, it is called the Bodhisattva Treasury.
These constitute the Three Piṭakas.
What are the Three Piṭakas?
They are the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka, and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
The Śrāvaka-piṭaka is so called because one hears it from others. Why is this?
Because one hears its sound.
The Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka refers to those who, by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, attain this state through the exhaustion of causes and conditions.
The Bodhisattva-piṭaka refers to those who enter into immeasurable dharmas and naturally achieve buddhahood.
As for those śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, that which constitutes the Tripiṭaka does not belong to the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
When this Dharma is taught, each of those who possess the Tripiṭaka attains that which corresponds to their own practice.
Why is this so? When this Dharma is taught, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas each attain their respective practices; therefore, it is called the Tripiṭaka.
Those who have attained the Dharma of a bodhisattva possess the Tripitaka. Why is this?
Because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not depart from the Buddha-dharma.
"Furthermore, there are three types of training in the Piṭakas. What are these three?
There is the training of the Śrāvaka, the training of the Pratyekabuddha, and the training of the Bodhisattva."
Those who study as śrāvakas do so because they possess a means of deliverance and seek only their own enlightenment.
Those who study as pratyekabuddhas are said to be those of middle capacity; they lack great compassion (mahākaruṇā).
The Dharma of the Bodhisattva cannot be measured, because they have entered the Dharma-body and because they employ great compassion.
Śrāvakas do not study the matters of Pratyekabuddhas, nor do they understand the matters of Pratyekabuddhas.
Pratyekabuddhas do not study the affairs of bodhisattvas, nor do they fully comprehend the affairs of bodhisattvas.
A bodhisattva knows that what is studied by śrāvakas is not to be taken as a source of joy; he harbors no expectations therein, nor does he seek liberation through it.
He likewise knows that what is studied by pratyekabuddhas is not to be taken as a source of joy, nor does he seek liberation through it.
And he knows the training of a bodhisattva, delighting in that which is to be learned and finding joy therein, because one shall attain liberation by means of it.
He manifests as a śrāvaka to teach and transform others through their practice; it is the same for pratyekabuddhas.
Because this is what the bodhisattva creates, it is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
It is like using a vessel to hold lapis lazuli; because of the lapis lazuli, the vessel also takes on the color of lapis lazuli.
When a bodhisattva has attained entry into the treasury, they do not depart from the Buddha in whatever dharmas they perceive.
When a bodhisattva has attained the treasury, all the dharmas they perceive are seen entirely as the Buddha-dharma.
The Bodhisattva has nothing among all dharmas that he does not study.
Why is this? Because there is no divergent view; all dharmas are exactly as the Buddha has realized them.
As for this Bodhisattva-piṭaka, it contains immeasurable numbers of teachings regarding the unfordable realms. Why is this?
Because it is free from increase or decrease.

Inconceivable light illuminates all darkness; that which is performed possesses the benefit of wisdom without limit, entering into omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) such that there is nowhere it does not penetrate.
To study this is truly to study, for by entering into the treasury of all things, one thereby enters into great wisdom (*mahājñāna*).
“Mahājñāna” means infinite wisdom; by means of it, those who have not yet entered are caused to enter.

At that time, after Mañjuśrī had explained the matters of the treasury to the bodhisattvas, he further expounded upon the three points regarding the adamantine practice of the wheel of the non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*).
When this was said, all who heard it attained this realization, and yet that wheel did not turn at all.
"The wheel of the *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) has no expectations toward anything; its mind is without differentiation."
Why is this? Because they do not dwell upon good or evil.

They study the Dharma with an impartial mind, viewing all Buddha-fields with equal vision, neither clinging to their beauty nor their ugliness, for they regard all Buddhas as equal and without distinction.
That wheel penetrates everywhere without exception.
Why is this? Because it does not destroy the Dharma-body.
For this reason, it is called the wheel of the irreversible (avaivartika) Dharma.
That wheel has no point of interruption. Why is this?
Because there is no dualistic mind.
As for that wheel, it is as it is seen. Why is this so?
Because it brings about Buddhahood through the Wheel of Dharma,
it is called the irreversible wheel of dharma (*avaivartika-dharmacakra*).
Those who follow this irreversible wheel are all liberated from all conceptualizations.
Those who believe this shall all become like the Buddha, for there are not two things.

They are liberated from what is taught through a single matter, just as the Tathāgata is liberated by means thereof. That liberation is without conceptualization and free from conceptualization; therefore, among all phenomena, where there is conceptualization, there is no liberation.
Why is this? Because liberation is non-dual.
For what reason?
Because there is no body, speech, or mind. Why is this so?
That which is liberated does not arise from body, speech, or mind; therefore, it is called liberation.
One who acts in this way does so from within themselves and not by following another; therefore, it is called the wheel of the *avaivartika*.
This wheel does not revolve through form. Why is this?
Because its nature is spontaneous, feeling,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness likewise do not arise. Why is this?
Because consciousness is spontaneous,
all phenomena likewise do not undergo transformation. Why is this so?
Because the Dharma-body has no turning,
it is called the irreversible wheel (*avaivartika-cakra*).
As for that wheel, its entry is without limit.
Why is this? Because there is no interruption.
That wheel is likewise without attachment and without interruption.
Why is this? Because that wheel has no gate. For what reason?
Because the mind is non-dual,
that truth likewise does not undergo transformation. Why is this so?
Because it is ineffable,
there is likewise no one who can understand that wheel. Why is this?
Furthermore, since it possesses no sound, how could one perceive its form?
Thus, regarding the truth that liberation can be attained through emptiness, none are able to reach it.
It is, for example, like space, which enters everywhere.
Why is it that there is nowhere it does not enter?
Because it is liberated from its origin.
That wheel is both able to move and able to walk.
What is meant by "walking" and what is meant by "stepping"?
It is like a diamond drill piercing through various jewels.
How can one pierce through that Dharma?
It is as if one were to bore through all things with emptiness; for this reason, the Dharma is called "the state of non-conceptualization," and it is therefore the Vajra. Why is this so?
Because it pierces through all that is sought;
the wishless (*apraṇihita*) is like a diamond drill that pierces all that has not yet been liberated so as to bring about liberation.
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is like a diamond; it empties all that is disturbed by means of the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The Tathāgata is like a diamond, completely piercing through all that is non-existent.
His liberation is like a diamond, surpassing all those who are not liberated.
Nirvāṇa is the vision of all dharmas as they are by nature.

When Mañjuśrī was preaching this wheel of the Dharma of the avaivartika for the sake of the bodhisattvas, all those bodhisattvas attained the Rāvikusuma samādhi, which in the Han language is called "Flower of Sunlight."

Having attained this samādhi, from every single hair-pore of that bodhisattva’s body, hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light are emitted. From each ray of light, one perceives hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas seated; each of these Buddhas proceeds to other lands to seek the path of Buddhahood and go forth to teach and transform beings.
At dawn the next day, King Ajātaśatru dispatched a messenger to Mañjuśrī, saying:
"I pray that you will deign to come at this time out of compassion for me.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa was about to enter the city with five hundred bhikṣus to beg for alms; however, halfway along the road, he thought it was still too early and turned back. Returning with the bhikṣus, he went to visit Mañjuśrī and arrived at his usual dwelling, standing outside the gate.
Mañjuśrī asked Mahākāśyapa,
"Where do you intend to go this morning?
To which he replied:
"I wish to go on almsround.
Mañjuśrī then said to Mahākāśyapa,
"I shall now go on almsround with you."
Mahākāśyapa then said:
"The offering has already been fully completed. Why is this so?..."
"It is by means of the Dharma that one arrives here, not for the sake of food.
Mañjuśrī said to Mahākāśyapa and the bhikṣus:
"One should arrive together at this point; it should be done both for the sake of the Dharma and for the sake of food."
"Why is this? It is because we do not lose the Dharma now, nor do we cause the food to be lost; thus, by uniting the two, we make them one.
Mahākāśyapa then replied:
"We shall always endure hunger and abstain from food; we must listen to this Dharma. Why is this?
For it is from this that each and every profound teaching is constantly heard."
Mahākāśyapa then asked again:
"Are you eating today together with the various mahāsattvas?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"The place where one now eats is such that the person neither leaves birth and death, nor enters nirvana; they neither transcend the affairs of desire, nor do they realize the Way."
"In the place where it is eaten, that food neither increases nor decreases; likewise, regarding all dharmas, there is nothing to be grasped and nothing to be relinquished.
Mahākāśyapa said, "One who practices such giving performs the supreme, boundless giving."
He then said,
“Yes, I accept your request.
Mañjuśrī then thought to himself:
"I shall now enter the city; my actions must be such as to move others like the transformations of a Buddha.
As he formed this thought, he immediately attained the samādhi known as "That Which Is Capable of Moving All."

At that time, the lands of the Śāṭha river were as level as a mirror; all mounds, ruins, mountains, and hills vanished from sight. His radiance reached everywhere, and for those suffering in the hells, their agonies were dispelled and they all attained peace and security.
In this land, at that time, all people were entirely free from lust, anger, and ignorance; they had no envy, no arrogance, and no malicious intent.
At that time, all people possessed hearts of loving-kindness, looking upon one another as they would their own fathers or mothers.

At that moment, the earth shook in six ways; the devas of the desire realm and the devas of the form realm made offerings to Mañjuśrī with a hundred kinds of musical performances, while raining down celestial flowers that scattered over him.

From the place where Mañjuśrī was staying, all the way to the city gates, they completely prepared and adorned the area. They tied various flowers together to form a lattice path running along both sides of the road, scattered famous and extraordinary blossoms over the entire ground, and draped curtains made of the most exquisite jewels over them.
The road was six zhang and three chi wide, with balustrades on both sides; it was adorned with trees fashioned from various jewels, arranged in rows along both edges of the path.
Then, cords made of jewels were used to bind the various trees together, linking them one after another.
From each single tree, a fragrance wafted in all four directions for forty *li*.
Between every two trees, a pond was miraculously manifested, its perimeter entirely enclosed by various precious gems serving as a barrier, adorned with *vaiḍūrya* crystal.
The sand of that water is entirely gold.
The water possesses the eight qualities of taste, and all manner of flowers grow within it; wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks frolic and play amidst them.
Beneath each tree, directly above its roots, there was a pedestal made of various jewels; upon each pedestal were incense burners fashioned from precious gems, all burning famous incenses.
On each mound were one hundred maidens, each holding a lotus flower and bearing sandalwood incense of renowned fragrance.
When Mañjuśrī entered this samādhi, his majestic spiritual power manifested transformations beyond measure.
Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, and said to Mahākāśyapa:
"Please go on ahead; I shall follow behind. Why is this?..."
"Because he is senior in years and because he was already a śramaṇa under previous Buddhas,
for these reasons he ought to stand at the head. Mahākāśyapa then replied:
“Those dharmas likewise have neither before nor after; they do not calculate years and ages to determine who is senior or junior.
Mañjuśrī said, “One should practice [the Dharma] and thereby be called venerable and senior.”
Mahākāśyapa replied:
"Wisdom is the most venerable.
One who has studied extensively is the most venerable."
"In whatever one does, to do so with reverence is itself the highest.
To seek to know the conduct of all people is itself the highest.
Mahākāśyapa spoke again:
“Mañjuśrī also possesses wisdom; his inquiries are complete, and in whatever he does, he understands the conduct of all people. For these reasons, he should be honored.”
Mahākāśyapa spoke again:
"If we consider our age now, he is likewise great and likewise venerable; therefore, he should take the place of honor, while I would gladly remain behind."
I now wish to speak a parable; I only pray that you will listen.

If it is the cub of a lion, its courage, spirit, and strength may not yet equal those of the great beast; yet though small, it partakes of the scent of the great one, and among all the birds and beasts, there are none who do not feel terror upon smelling its odor.

It is like a great elephant with six tusks that is sixty years of age; if a person were to bind this elephant with a rope made of leather, the cub of a lion, upon smelling the scent of that leather rope at its location, would cause the great elephant to bolt and run into the mountains.

Although the Bodhisattva’s resolve has not yet perfected its power and majesty, it is beyond the reach of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; all Māras are stirred with alarm, shrinking their waists in fear.
When the lion’s cub sees the large one and roars, whatever it may do, its heart is neither afraid nor terrified. Why is this?
They were even more filled with joy.
Now, when such a bodhisattva sees the Buddha performing his deeds, their mind is neither afraid nor terrified. Why is this?
"Having become doubly joyful,
I now also dare to act in this same way.
Śāriputra said:
"If one were to calculate who is more venerable—whether it be a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha—it is the one who has resolved their mind toward bodhisattvahood who is truly venerable. Why is this so?"
"Whatever is sought arises from the mind of the Bodhisattva.
Mahākāśyapa said, "Therefore, Mañjuśrī is the most honored; he should indeed take the lead, while we follow behind him."
Mañjuśrī went at the front, followed by the bodhisattvas; the śrāvakas also followed behind them as they set out upon the road.

The heavens rained down flowers, the earth shook in six ways, and the devas above provided entertainment with music. At that moment, a radiance shone forth such that nothing remained unilluminated, and they arrived at Rājagṛha.
Before he had yet entered the city gates, King Ajātaśatru heard that Mañjuśrī had arrived that morning, accompanied by twenty-two thousand five hundred bodhisattvas and five hundred bhikṣus.
The king thought to himself:
"I have prepared provisions for five hundred people; how shall I now provide for them?
Where shall they sit?"
At that moment, the celestial king named Citta-viśrāma, together with the noble yakṣa named Suvarṇa-śūla, arrived and met with King Ajātaśatru, saying:
"Do not fear, do not be anxious, and do not consider this difficult."
He replied: "How could one not consider this difficult?
Then he answered:
“Mañjuśrī has arrived, having manifested the boundless wisdom of *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) and being fully endowed with the radiance of merit.

By virtue of his supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), if one were to give a single meal to Mañjuśrī, he could satisfy the hunger of every person throughout the trichiliocosm; yet that food would not be exhausted, even as they continued to seek it.”
Why should these twenty-three thousand people be a cause for concern?
Therefore, do not regard this as difficult. Why is that?
"Now everything is acceptable and fully sufficient.
Mañjuśrī’s merit is most sublime and inexhaustible. King Ajātaśatru was immediately filled with joy;

his heart leaped with double delight, and he prepared what was to be done. Taking up music and carrying flowers and incense, he went out in person to welcome Mañjuśrī and the others, and they entered the palace together.

At that time, among the bodhisattvas, there was one named Samantadarśin (Universal Vision), who, at the command of Mañjuśrī, instructed Samantāloka to prepare the site so that it could accommodate those who were coming.
That bodhisattva received the instruction and, looking out in the four directions at that very moment, everything was immediately prepared.
Within the assembly, there was another bodhisattva named Dharmāgata, who, having received the command, provided the seats.

Immediately upon receiving the instruction, in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, twenty-three thousand couches and seats appeared; they were covered with cushions of various colors, and fine pearls, exquisite embroidery, and fabrics of diverse hues were all spread upon them.
Mañjuśrī and all the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas took their seats.
King Ajātaśatru approached Mañjuśrī and said:
"The offerings we have prepared are very few; please bear with us for a moment while we now wish to provide further preparations."
He then replied:
"What has been done is sufficient for oneself; do not weary your mind further.
King Vaiśravaṇa, together with his household and attendants, all came to pay their respects, and they all served him with reverence at his side.

Śakra Devānām Indra himself, together with his chief queen named Śūryā and the celestial maidens, all held famous incense as an offering, scattering it over Mañjuśrī, the various bodhisattvas, and the community of bhikṣus.
Those bodhisattvas were not moved by the celestial maidens, nor by the music, nor by the flowers and incense.
Then Brahmā himself transformed into a young brahmin, exceedingly handsome and upright; holding a fan, he stood to the right of Mañjuśrī and attended him, fanning him.
All the sons of the Brahmā gods likewise attended upon the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Bhikṣus, standing to their right and serving them while holding fans.

The Dragon King Anavatapta, situated above the assembly in the void where he was invisible to anyone, held a string of pearls that hung down like a banner; from this string of pearls, water flowed downward, possessing the eight qualities of taste. Whatever one desired to do, one should take this water entirely.
Before each member of the assembly of Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattvas, and the bhikṣus, there hung a pendant pearl from which water issued forth, providing everything that each person required.
King Ajātaśatru thought again:
"Those who have come to this assembly do not carry bowls; with what vessel should they now eat?
Mañjuśrī, knowing the king's thoughts, spoke:

"A Bodhisattva does not carry an alms-bowl when traveling; however, while at the place where he eats, he brings the bowl to mind, and the bowl spontaneously comes from that buddha-field and rests in his hand."
Ajātaśatru asked Mañjuśrī again:
"From which buddha-fields have all these bodhisattvas come to this place?
What are the names of their Buddhas?"
Mañjuśrī then said:
"The name of that buddha-field is Śatadhvaja, and the name of its Buddha is Viśuddhaśrī. He has come from there to this place to partake of your meal."
"Why is this? It is because they have come wishing to hear the Dharma and to listen to the doubts of the Venerable One.
The bodhisattvas thought of their alms bowls, and at that moment the bowls flew there; they arrived in formation at Lake Anavatapta, where each was purified by sprinkling and filled with water.
The nāga ladies all came bearing twenty-three thousand bowls, presenting them to the bodhisattvas of the Ghoṣadatta land, placing one into the hand of each individual.
Ajātaśatru remained in attendance upon Mañjuśrī, and Mañjuśrī then said to Ajātaśatru:
"Distribute the food.
He immediately followed these instructions and distributed it everywhere; yet the food did not diminish, remaining as it was before.
Ajātaśatru spoke again:
"The food has been distributed everywhere, yet it remains as it was before, without any deficiency. Mañjuśrī said:
"Is it now exhausted?
he asked, and the reply was:
"It is not exhausted."
“The reason it has not been exhausted is because of your doubt.

After the bodhisattvas had finished their meal, they held up their bowls and leaped into the air, where they remained arranged in rows; neither did they fall to the ground, nor did they waver or shake.
Ajātaśatru asked again:
"How does this bowl remain?
Upon what does it depend?"
Mañjuśrī replied,
“This bowl abides in the same manner as that in which your doubt abides.
Ajātaśatru spoke again:
"This bowl also has no place of abiding; it is neither on the ground, nor does it rely upon anything, nor does it have any location.
Mañjuśrī then said:
"If even doubt has no place of abiding, then all dharmas are likewise like this bowl—having no place of abiding and no place of falling."
When the meal was finished, Ajātaśatru took a small stool and sat before Mañjuśrī, personally declaring:
"I pray that you will resolve my doubts."
Mañjuśrī then said: "Even Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges could not resolve this doubt for you.
At that moment, Ajātaśatru was struck with terror; he fell from his seat like a great tree crashing to the ground.
Mahākāśyapa said to Ajātaśatru:
"Do not be afraid; have no fear. Why is this?
“Mañjuśrī has entered into the profound *upāyakauśalya*; for this reason he speaks thus.
You may ask him at your leisure. Then Ajātaśatru asked:
“Regarding what you have just said, even Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges could not explain the doubts I harbor.
Mañjuśrī replied, “Virtuous one,
you believe that a Buddha can be perceived through the causes and conditions of the mind.”
The King replied:
"It is not by means of the mind, for it arises from the mind.
[He asked: "Can the Buddha be seen?"
The King said, "No.
[The interlocutor asked,] "Can one see the Buddha by means of having a mind?"
The king said, “No. [The interlocutor asked:
“Birth-and-death and liberation—these are two distinct matters; by maintaining these, does one become a Buddha?”
The King said, "No.
[The interlocutor asked,] "And yet, is there not a Dharma teaching that follows from this Dharma?"
The king said, "No.
[The interlocutor asked: "Can one who practices such a method provide a definitive explanation?"
The King said, "No.
[The Buddha continued,] "For this reason, I say that even if one were to encounter Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, one who harbors such doubt could never explain it."
"Why is that? If someone were to say, 'I am able to defile empty space with dust,' would they truly be able to do so?
The King said:
"No. "If someone were to say, 'I can remove the defilement of space,' could they actually remove it?"
The king said, "I cannot. Mañjuśrī said:
“The Buddha knows that all phenomena are entirely like empty space. Why is this?
Because they are liberated from their origin; furthermore, he does not perceive any phenomenon to have an origin, nor does he perceive one who is liberated.”
"For this reason, I say that if the King harbors such doubt, it is not something that even Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges could resolve.
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
"The Tathāgata does not perceive an internal or external mind; what, then, could there be to cause doubt?"
Why is this so? Because all dharmas are fundamentally and entirely liberated.
For what reason, then, would there still be doubt?
Mañjuśrī spoke again:

“One who is fundamentally liberated no longer clings even to emptiness; because all dharmas are originally non-existent, it is called liberation. Furthermore, it is not spontaneous, not something accomplished, and nothing that can be perceived.”

All phenomena possess both existence and non-existence; because all phenomena are without anything seen, they are invisible. All phenomena are called silence; this is what is meant by "perception that cannot be known."
All phenomena are without conceptualization; having transcended spontaneity, they are thus fully passed beyond.
"All phenomena" refers to the severance of birth and death.
"All phenomena have no location" refers to the absence of aspiration.
All dharmas are without aspiration, because there is neither birth nor death.
All dharmas are without attachment, because they are pure.
All dharmas are entirely pure, because they are fundamentally and internally as well as externally pure.
All phenomena are without a counterpart, meaning they have no companion.
All phenomena have no companion, meaning they are of one mind.
All phenomena are of one mind, meaning they are liberated.
All phenomena have no limit, because there is nothing to be severed.
All phenomena have no boundaries, because there is no crossing over.
That all phenomena cannot be seen as something crossed over is because their manifestations are diverse.
Regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*), that which is called "the differentiation of what is produced" refers to seeking wisdom, meaning that one cannot attain peace.
That all phenomena are impermanent means that there is no dualistic mind.
That all phenomena are entirely peaceful means that they have transcended purity.
All dharmas are fully resolved, because there is nothing to be sought.
There is no dharma of spontaneity, because a self cannot be apprehended.
All dharmas are free from doubt, because they are internally tranquil.
How marvelous are all phenomena, for they are without truth.
All phenomena are quiescent, for they are utterly level.
All phenomena are without self, for there is nothing that belongs to a self.
All phenomena are without remainder, because they are liberated.
All phenomena do not undergo transformation or transmigration, because they are devoid of conceptualization.
All phenomena are entirely characterized by faith, because there is neither attachment nor cessation.
All phenomena have a single flavor, because they are liberated.
All phenomena are peaceful and secure, because they are devoid of conceptualization.
All phenomena are devoid of conceptualization, because they are indestructible.
All phenomena are entirely empty, for they transcend all seeking.
All phenomena are without aspiration, for they refer to the three realms.
All phenomena sever the three realms, meaning they do not cling to the past, the future, or the present.
"All dharmas are like nirvāṇa, meaning that which has arisen is as if it had not arisen.
Mañjuśrī said to Ajātaśatru,
"There is nothing that arises."
"Is that which is unarisen capable of being purified?
The King replied, "No."
Mañjuśrī said: "The Buddha knows that all dharmas are like nirvāṇa; therefore, one cannot be liberated from one's doubts. Why is this so?"
One should dwell in direct observation of all phenomena (*dharma*).

Having observed all phenomena, one neither grasps nor rejects them, nor does one find any place of rest within phenomena; because all phenomena are without a place of rest, one is at peace. Being at peace, one has no doubt. Having no doubt, one performs no further action. To perform no further action means to have no master. Within this state, one should cultivate such patience.
Why is this? Because one does not conceive of oneself as "using" various dharmas, one endures that all dharmas are unconditioned—that is, what can be done and what cannot be done.
All dharmas are without action; because there is no action and no agent, this is *nirvāṇa*.
Those who believe this regard it as equal liberation, wherein there is neither increase nor decrease.

Because all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, there is no agency; yet that which can act is entirely fundamentally non-existent. That which is fundamentally non-existent is neither "is" nor "is not"; therefore, fundamental non-existence has no differentiation.
Having already attained faith without distinction, all doubts have been completely exhausted.
That eye is neither defiled nor pure; because the nature of the eye is thus, it is fundamentally non-existent. Because its fundamental non-existence is its very nature, it is called "the eye."

The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise neither defiled nor pure; for the mind is by its very nature such that it is fundamentally non-existent, and because it is fundamentally non-existent and natural, it is called "mind."
Form (*rūpa*) is also originally non-existent; original non-existence is the very nature of form.

Feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are likewise neither defiled nor pure. Consciousness is by its very nature originally non-existent; because it is originally non-existent by its very nature, it is called "consciousness."

All dharmas are entirely without defilement and without purity; all dharmas are naturally and fundamentally non-existent. Because they are naturally and fundamentally non-existent, they are called "all dharmas.
That mind is likewise invisible, and form cannot be grasped or maintained.
Why is this? It is like a magical illusion, which cannot be said to function by means of the internal, nor can it be said to function by means of the external. Why is that?
Because it is fundamentally pure, it is without defilement.
That which is the fundamental mind is neither grasped, nor increased, nor troubled, nor distressed, nor sorrowful.

Those who hear this Dharma have no doubts; it is because their fundamental nature differs and their thoughts differ that defilement arises. One should know that while the fundamental nature differs and thoughts differ, that which does not exist cannot be made to exist.
Your Majesty, you should not harbor such thoughts.
It is as if someone were to say, "I can make empty space dirty with smoke or dust. By doing so, could one actually make empty space dirty?
The King said, “No. Mañjuśrī said:
"Since that mind is fundamentally pure, lust, anger, and delusion have no way to enter; what more need be said?
It is like the void manifesting five things:
first, ash; second, dust; third, smoke; fourth, mist; and fifth, clouds. Although these can all be seen, one cannot say that they create defilement within the void."
Just as when people say, "This was done by me" or "This was not done by me," there arise lust, anger, and delusion;
yet within the fundamental nature of the mind, neither defilement nor doubt is produced.
Why is this so? Because the mind that has already arisen cannot prevent the subsequent mind from arising;
and the subsequent mind that arises does not seek out the preceding mind.
The present mind, too, has no location.
The wise person who has already understood this activity is without expectation; because there is nothing to be expected, it is the mark of purity.
All dharmas are without defilement, without anything that is not illuminated, without arising, and without location.
This lack of location is the birthplace of the Buddha; "birthplace" refers to all dharmas, and because all dharmas are the birthplace, they cannot be described.

As for those who possess wisdom, there is no liberation from any phenomena; they take the Dharma as liberation from all doubts. Because there is nothing that exists and no phenomenon by which one is delivered, doubt belongs to the Dharmakāya. Therefore, it is said that the Dharmakāya enters into all phenomena without exception, yet one does not perceive the Dharmakāya as having anything into which it enters.
Why is this? All phenomena are the Dharma-body.
Since all phenomena are equal, the Dharma-body is likewise equal; therefore, it is called "that which the Dharma-body enters."
When these words were spoken, King Ajātaśatru attained the patient acceptance of joyful faith; he then leaped for joy and said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"Please resolve my doubts.
Mañjuśrī then replied,
"This is a great doubt."
The Dharma that has been preached has no fundamental basis; from where, then, could doubt arise?
From what source could one hear of doubt?
King Ajātaśatru then said:
"Having received great grace, I have attained a slight recovery.
Now that my life is at its end, I do not worry about not reaching Nirvāṇa. Mañjuśrī said:
"That which the King hopes for has no fundamental basis. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are fundamentally nirvāṇa; therefore, nothing is produced."
King Ajātaśatru then rose from his seat, took up a fine, exquisite cloth worth hundreds of thousands of millions, and held it around the body of Mañjuśrī.
At that moment, Mañjuśrī’s body vanished; the cloth remained suspended in mid-air, and while his voice could be heard, his form could not be seen. Then, from that sound, he spoke:
"If you see Mañjuśrī’s body, O King, you will see your own doubts."
"One does not regard one who views with doubt as one who sees all dharmas; is it not so according to what has been seen?
Again, a voice was heard from the sky, saying:
"O King, regarding that which you have seen, take this cloth and give it to him."
Next, there was a bodhisattva seated at the place where Mañjuśrī sat, named Prāptottarapraṇidhāna.
Ajātaśatru again wished to take this cloth and offer it to him.
The Bodhisattva said:
"Regarding those who seek liberation through nirvana, I do not receive anything from them, nor do I accept anything that ordinary people possess."
Why is this? Because ordinary people do not accept it due to mundane affairs.

Nor do they seek anything to accept from Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas, nor do they seek anything to accept from the Dharma of the Tathāgata. It is because one neither approaches these dharmas nor departs from these dharmas that I accept this thing.
The giver had no dualistic mind, and the receiver likewise had no dualistic mind; therefore it is said that "that which is received surpasses liberation.
The King then wished to place his robe upon the Bodhisattva, but suddenly he vanished and his whereabouts were unknown. Only his voice was heard, not his form, as he spoke:
"To whichever body he manifests himself, give the robe to him."
After that bodhisattva had sat down, there was another bodhisattva named Sarvamāyādarśana,
to whom King Ajātaśatru again offered this robe.
The Bodhisattva said:
"If there are those who conceive of others as having a self, I do not accept things from them; nor do I accept things from those who are defiled, nor from those who have attained liberation."
Nor does he receive these things from one whose mind is in meditative concentration, nor from one whose mind is distracted;
nor does he receive these things from one possessed of wisdom, nor from one devoid of wisdom.
Ajātaśatru then threw his robe onto the couch; the bodhisattva immediately vanished, and he heard the voice again but could not see its form, which said:
"To whoever appears, give this robe."
Now, at the place where this bodhisattva sat, there was another bodhisattva named Adṛṣṭamāyā-yāvan-nirvāṇa (Not Seeing Illusion up to Nirvana).
Ajātaśatru held up his robe with his hands and approached him, saying:
"The one who sat above has already departed; you may take it, O virtuous one."
The Bodhisattva said:
"If there is one who is attached to self or to others, I will not accept such a thing.

One who is not attached to the five aggregates, the four great elements, or the six sense bases, and who is likewise unattached to the Buddha, unattached to the Dharma, and unattached to the Sangha—[to such a person I shall give it]."
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are without attachment.
King Ajātaśatru then took his robe and wished to place it upon the Bodhisattva; however, at that moment, he did not appear. Only his voice was heard, but his form remained invisible, as he spoke:
"To whoever appears here, give him a robe.
Now, there was a bodhisattva seated in that assembly named Sihakama;
Ajātaśatru then offered a robe to him.
The Bodhisattva said: "I do not accept things from one who lacks vision.

Now, you have resolved upon the mind of a Bodhisattva and maintain a mind like that of a Bodhisattva; your mind is equal toward all phenomena and likewise equal toward all Buddha-dharmas. It neither grasps nor rejects; it has neither doubt nor suspicion regarding all phenomena. It does not conceive of phenomena as having a self, nor does it conceive of phenomena as having anything to be liberated from. Only if you possess such an intention shall I accept this thing."
King Ajātaśatru then placed his robe upon the Bodhisattva; at that moment, the Bodhisattva did not manifest his form, but only a voice was heard, saying:
"To whoever appears, give the robe."
Now, seated next to that bodhisattva was another bodhisattva named Samadhi-kausuma.
Ajātaśatru held out his robe, wishing to offer it to him,
but that bodhisattva said:
"If there is such a samādhi that is free from doubt, then one may accept those objects.
Only when one fully knows through this fundamental samādhi that all dharmas are without anything to be relinquished do I accept these objects."
King Ajātaśatru then took the robe and placed it upon him; immediately, he vanished from sight, and only his voice was heard saying:
"To whoever appears here, give this robe."
Next in that assembly was a bodhisattva named Mātrā-vīrya, who said:
"All sounds, syllables, and voices are unobtainable; only when one acts in this manner shall I accept this offering."
King Ajātaśatru again took his robe and placed it over him; however, the figure immediately vanished from sight, and only its voice was heard saying:
"To whoever appears before you, give this robe."
Now, seated next to him was a bodhisattva named Vigatarajomala (Free from the Stain of Activity).
Ajātaśatru wished to offer his robe to him,
but that bodhisattva said:

"He does not think, 'I am giving my body to him,' nor does he think, 'There is someone taking from me,' nor does he think, 'There will be some benefit for me. Only when these thoughts are absent does he accept that object."
The king again placed his robe upon him, but immediately the figure vanished; only his voice was heard saying:
"To whoever appears before you, give this robe."
Now, in the seat next to him was a bodhisattva named Dharmavikurvaṇarāja.
Ajātaśatru again offered his robe to him.
That bodhisattva said:

"If you manifest as a śrāvaka without entering parinirvāṇa, and manifest as a pratyekabuddha without entering parinirvāṇa, and neither abide in saṃsāra nor reach nirvāṇa, then I shall accept your gift."
King Ajātaśatru then placed his robe upon it;
suddenly, it vanished, and only its voice was heard saying:
"To whoever appears here, give this robe."
In this manner, he gave a robe to each one of them, yet they were not seen at that time; even their beds, tables, and seats did not appear. Again, he heard their voices say:
"Give the robes to those who have appeared."
Ajātaśatru said to Mahākāśyapa:
"I have heard from the Buddha that you are especially venerable; I now offer this robe to you, and I pray that you will accept it."
Mahākāśyapa was unwilling to accept it.
"Why is this? Because my lust, anger, and delusion have not yet been completely eradicated, I cannot accept it."

Furthermore, it is not apart from the absence of wisdom, nor apart from evil, nor apart from the knowledge of suffering; it is neither practiced nor exhausted, neither guided nor taken as the realization of exhaustion; there is no mindfulness of the Path, nor is there any perception of the Tathāgata, nor hearing of the Dharma, nor association with the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus; there is no arising of insight, nor purification of the eye, nor is there any action performed by means of consciousness abiding anywhere.
"One who gives me things cannot possess great virtue, nor can they attain noble liberation.
Mahākāśyapa said,
"If you form the intention to be like me, then I shall accept it."
King Ajātaśatru then placed his robe over it, but at that moment he could not see it; he heard only its voice saying:
"To whoever appears, give the robe."
He then proceeded to give the robes one by one to the bhikṣus, yet he did not see a single one of them.
He searched for all five hundred men, but none appeared;
he heard only their voices saying, "To whoever appears, give the robe."
King Ajātaśatru reflected deeply within himself:
"If all the bodhisattvas and the community of bhikṣus have perished, to whom shall I give these robes?
He returned them to his principal consort, but she too was nowhere to be seen.
At that moment, King Ajātaśatru immediately attained samādhi; he saw no forms, nor did he see women, nor men, nor boys, nor girls, nor walls, nor trees, nor houses, nor cities.
There still remained a lingering thought, namely the notion of a self-body; all perceptions of form ceased.
Then he again heard a voice say:
"Just as one perceives all that is seen, so should one perceive one's own doubt."
Just as one views doubt, so too should one view all phenomena.
One should view what is seen as being without seeing; one should view the phenomenon of non-seeing—this is called viewing phenomena.
"Whatever one sees, one shall give it to you.

When the King saw nothing further, he took the robe and intended to put it on himself, yet he no longer saw his own body; his mind, consciousness, and all conceptualizations had ceased to exist. This is called being liberated from perception and liberated from doubt.
Then, emerging from samādhi, he saw that the assembly of bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, and all their various officials and attendants were exactly as they had been before.
Ajātaśatru spoke again to Mañjuśrī:
"I did not see any of these gathered assemblies while I was within [the samādhi]."
Mañjuśrī said: "As for the place of your doubt, it lies within this assembly.
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
“Did you see the assembly?
Ajātaśatru replied,
“I saw them.”
“How do you see them? “Just as I see my own doubts, I see the assembly in this same way.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
“Did you see the assembly?
Ajātaśatru replied,
“I saw them.”
"How so? "Just as I perceive my own doubts, I perceive the assembly in this same way.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
“What is meant by ‘seeing doubt’?
“It is as when I, belonging to this assembly, do not see those who are gathered; thus, one sees neither within nor without. Mañjuśrī said:
“Have you heard what the Buddha said— that those who commit rebellious and evil deeds shall enter the great niraya?
The King replied,
“I have heard.”
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
"O King, do you know for yourself whether you shall enter hell?
Ajātaśatru asked in return:
"When that Buddha attained Buddhahood, were there any who went from the heavens to the hells?
Were there any who found peace and were destined for Nirvana?
Mañjuśrī then replied:
"No," the King said,
"because I know that all phenomena are entirely empty."
Why is this so? The hells are already empty, and the heavens of the gods above are also empty.
All dharmas are incapable of being destroyed or decayed; therefore, one enters the Dharma-body.
The Dharma-body exists neither in the heavens, nor among humans, nor in the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts.

Even those who commit transgressions do not depart from the Dharma-body; the bodies of those who commit such transgressions are entirely encompassed within the Dharma-body, for the root of all transgressions is the very root of all dharmas.
That which has already gone and that which is yet to come have no going or coming;
likewise, all dharmas have no going or coming. One who knows this neither enters the hells, nor ascends to heaven, nor attains nirvāṇa.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
“The Buddha has spoken of the heinous crimes;
why do you now say they do not exist?”
The king then replied:
"I shall not contradict what the Buddha has said.
[The other asked: "In what way?"
The king said:
"The absence of self is the teaching of the Buddha.
To be truly without self means that there is no person; thus, there is neither one who commits a transgression nor one who undergoes punishment for it."
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Has the King now been liberated from doubt? He replied:
"From the very beginning they have been liberated,
and from the outset they have also been liberated. Mañjuśrī said,
"Is their doubt now exhausted?"
The King said:
"It has been exhausted since long ago.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"How does the assembly know whether the king has committed a heinous crime or is liberated from it?
The king replied,
"Because I am sustained by the Honored Dharma, they know that I have not committed a heinous crime."
"It is as if a bodhisattva, having already attained forbearance (*kṣānti*), takes upon himself all evils;
such is the bodhisattva’s gift of excellent vows. Nāgārjuna said to Ajātaśatru:
"Are all the heinous crimes purified by attaining this forbearance?"
The King said:
"All dharmas are entirely pure, for they are free from defilement;
these dharmas likewise cannot be defiled."
Why is this? Because that Way is free from any blemish or defilement.
Those who enter the way of great transgression do not depart from birth-and-death, nor do they perceive Nirvana.
"Why is this? Because that Way has no destination to which one may go, nor anything toward which one may draw near.
When these words were spoken, King Ajātaśatru immediately attained the patient acceptance of swift faith (*kṣiprādhimukti-kṣānti*).

Then those thirty-two people, in the presence of Mañjuśrī, all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and the five hundred ministers and subordinates all attained the stage of srotāpanna.
The people of Rājagṛha crowded the palace gates, desiring to see Mañjuśrī preach the Dharma.

At that moment, Mañjuśrī pointed to the ground with his big toe, and the palace walls and the earth all became made of lapis lazuli. Everyone outside could clearly see all the bodhisattvas and the community of bhikṣus within the palace; just as one sees one’s own reflection when looking into a mirror, what they beheld at that time was entirely distinct. All listened to the Dharma preached by Mañjuśrī, and eighty-four thousand people attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. Furthermore, five hundred people all resolved their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

After Mañjuśrī had preached the Dharma for the king, the members of the palace, and all the officials, establishing each of them in peace and security, he rose from his seat and, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and bhikṣus, departed through the palace gate.
King Ajātaśatru and the officials and attendants of the palace accompanied him on his way out.
Once outside the city gate, he saw a man beneath a tree who was crying out loudly, "I have killed my mother!"
When this person was about to attain liberation, Mañjuśrī manifested as a man traveling together with his parents.
His parents said:
"This is the correct path; you should proceed along it."
The son said,
"This is not the right path.
Thus he argued with his parents up to three times, and then he conceived the intention to kill them.

The one previously called the "Matricide" saw this person and killed his own parents; he then raised his voice from the sidelines and spoke to him. The transformed man who had killed his parents then confessed:
"What I have done is not recorded in the Dharma; I have perversely murdered my parents."
Then one of them thought:
"I have killed only my mother;
this man has killed both his father and mother, and thus his transgression is exceedingly grave."
"What you have received as a son is still but slight compared to mine.
The transformed person then said to one man:
"I shall go to where the Buddha is."
The Buddha is one to whom those with no refuge turn for refuge, and one who acts as a protector for those without protection.
As the Buddha has spoken, I shall receive his instruction and dare not transgress it.
As that teacher of men proceeded toward the Way, one person followed behind him, saying:
"Just as this man has received the Dharma, so shall I likewise."
"Even so, I still lament this.
They wept together as they proceeded.
Upon reaching the Buddha's dwelling, they prostrated themselves before him and stood there, then addressed him:
"I have committed an unrighteous act by falsely killing my parents.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
What you have said is most sincere and without deviation. Why is this?
Because you do not conceal the transgressions you have committed; even before the Tathāgata, you have spoken of matters as they truly are.
The Buddha then said, "Do not fear, do not be anxious; follow what I say.
The emanated person replied:
“As the Buddha has taught, we pray that you will compassionately grant us your protection.
The Buddha said:
“Return to the method of observing your own mind; examine the past, future, and present minds. Holding which mind did you kill your parents?”
The Buddha then spoke again:
"The past mind has already ceased and already perished; its location cannot be seen, nor can its whereabouts be seen.
The future mind cannot be described."
Why is this? Because that which has not yet arisen does not exist and has no being; thus, there is neither perception nor thought.

Even the present mind has no place of abiding; when the mind arises as intention, it immediately ceases. It does not aggregate or coalesce, nor can one know where it goes or from where it comes. Furthermore, one cannot know whether it is blue, red, white, yellow, or black.
The mind is invisible; it has no form, nor can it be grasped, nor does it have a companion—it is like a magical illusion.
Within the body, it cannot be seen inside, nor is it seen outside, nor is it seen in between.
The Buddha said:
"The mind cannot be seen through attachment, nor can it be seen through anger.
Whether one is lying down and seeing the mind in a dream, or whether one is acting or not acting, the mind has nothing to give and nothing to obtain."
"Because the mind is fundamentally pure, it is neither defiled nor is there anyone who purifies it.
The Buddha spoke again:
"That mind is neither here nor there; it is like an illusion, incapable of being grasped."
Why is this? Because there is no companion.

One who understands thus does not form such conceptions; they do not think of self or non-self, nor do they think of anything seen, nor do they think of anything abiding, [realizing that] all phenomena are quiescent yet have an agent.
Those who believe this will no longer undergo rebirth in the evil realms. Why is this?
Because they are free from defilement.
"Those mental phenomena are likewise neither produced nor attached to.
Then the emanated person said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Just as the Tathāgata attained Buddhahood through the Dharma-body, so now one should know it as the Buddha has taught.
With faith and without doubt, there is no agent and no one who undergoes retribution; there is nothing born and nothing extinguished.
"As with all dharmas, I vow and aspire to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha said,
"It shall be as you wish, my son."
At that moment, the transformed person appeared as a śramaṇa and addressed the Buddha:
"Regarding the crimes I committed by killing my father and mother, I have already been liberated from them and attained arhatship; I now wish to enter parinirvāṇa."
The Buddha said, "Go as you wish.
This manifested bhikṣu flew twenty zhang above the ground, and while in mid-air, he entered parinirvāṇa; fire issued from his body and consumed it.
When that matricide sees this person having entered parinirvāṇa and hears in full what the Tathāgata has taught, he thinks to himself:
"The deeds this man committed were most rebellious, yet now, having become a śramaṇa, he has attained liberation and entered parinirvāṇa."
"If my transgression were still permissible, why should I not take refuge in the Buddha? I too could reach this state.
He then stepped forward, prostrated before the Buddha, and declared:
"I have committed an unrighteous act; I have killed my own mother."
Now I take refuge with my very body.
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent!”
What you have spoken is most sincere and without deviation; what you have said accords with your words.
Having seen the Tathāgata, confess the transgressions you have committed without concealment.
Furthermore, contemplate the nature of the mind: considering the past, future, and present minds, which mind was it that killed its mother?
The past mind has already ceased and perished; it is neither external nor internal, and it has no location.
The future mind cannot be described; it has not yet arisen and does not yet exist, and it is likewise without thought or any object of thought.
The present mind likewise has no place of abiding; when the mind arises, it is immediately destroyed, neither accumulating nor reaching any destination, nor can its point of origin be seen.
That mind is neither blue, red, yellow, white, nor black; that mind has no form and is invisible, it cannot be grasped, and it cannot be heard.
Why is this? Because there is no sound.
It cannot be apprehended or attained, nor does it have any companion; it is like an illusion.
Nor does one perceive the body externally; it is not found internally either, nor is there any location for it in between.
That mind is likewise neither defiled, nor evil, nor subject to doubt.
That mind is without action, nor does it perform any action; it gives nothing away, nor does it obtain anything.
Because the mind is fundamentally pure, it is neither defiled nor is it pure.
That mind does not abide in either "is" or "is not.
If the mind is empty, it cannot be apprehended, nor does it have a companion.

The wise person does not conceive such notions; they neither create bondage nor create purity; they do not produce views, nor do they establish a locus, nor do they have any place of rest, nor do they cling to existence.
One whose mind is liberated is therefore without obstruction and does not take birth in evil realms. Why is this?
Because the nature of that mind has no attachment, it does not converge upon anything, nor does it abide in the realm of birth and death.
As for that one who had killed his mother, at that moment, from every single pore of his body, the fires of hell issued forth; the pain was beyond words, and he then declared:
"I now take refuge in the Tathāgata."
"May you, out of compassion, grant us protection so that we may attain peace and security.
Thereupon, the Buddha placed his golden hand upon the man's head; instantly the fire was extinguished and the suffering was relieved.
He then stepped forward, knelt down, and expressed his wish to become a śramaṇa.
The Buddha said,
"As you desire."
He then became a śramaṇa.

The Tathāgata taught him by means of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; he immediately attained the Dharma-eye, and by penetrating deeply into its meaning, he realized arhatship. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now I wish to enter parinirvāṇa."
The Buddha said, "As you wish.
He flew into the air to a height of one hundred and forty *zhang* above the ground, and from there, flames issued from his body, which he used to burn himself.
Hundreds of thousands of millions of devas all flew there to make offerings.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is truly venerable."
Why is this? It is so that those who have committed evil may attain liberation.
Who is it that is liberated?

Only the Buddha, or Mañjuśrī and the various bodhisattvas who have deeply entered the saṃnāhasaṃnaddha (the armor of great vows), know this matter; it is not something that arhats or pratyekabuddhas are capable of knowing within.
"If it is that which no one at all can reach or attain," the Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"that which is the realm of the Tathāgata is what the bodhisattva endures; it is not the stage of the arhat or the pratyekabuddha, nor is it that which any person at all can practice."
Why is this? If there is a person whose actions are different, they shall obtain a different result accordingly.
When you see those who commit offenses, you know they are destined for hell; yet I can cause them not to enter hell and instead reach Nirvana.
If it were as you know it, that there should be those who enter parinirvāṇa, I would know that I am destined for hell. Why?
Because you do not understand the conduct of all people.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Do you see that man who killed his mother as he enters parinirvāṇa?
He then replied:
"I have seen them," the Buddha said.
"This person has made offerings to five hundred Buddhas until they were exhausted, and from each and every Buddha, he heard that the fundamental nature of the mind is pure."
Why is this? Because now they hear this Dharma and attain parinirvāṇa.
Those who understand this profound Dharma and enter its subtlety will leap for joy, their hearts free from fear.
If one is misled by an evil teacher, or if their mind is not yet sufficient, they shall nevertheless be liberated from the offenses they have committed.
One who possesses faith that the Dharma is fundamentally pure will not fall into the evil realms.
"Why is this? Because there is no obstruction.
Then Mañjuśrī, together with the bodhisattvas, Mahākāśyapa, the community of bhikṣus, King Ajātaśatru, and his retinue of ministers and officials, came to where the Buddha was.
Śāriputra asked Ajātaśatru,
"Now that you have heard this, has your doubt been resolved? He replied:
"It is known through hearing. What is meant by 'hearing'?

When the Dharma is taught, there is nothing attained and nothing not attained; there is nothing grasped and nothing relinquished. Upon hearing this, from this moment forward, one shall be free from defilement."
At that time, Śāriputra asked the Buddha,
“How much of Ajātaśatru’s remaining karmic retribution still remains?
The Buddha said:
“The Dharma you have heard is like a single mustard seed that can exhaust the sins of Mount Sumeru.
Śāriputra asked the Buddha,
“Will King Ajātaśatru enter Niraya?”
“It is like a son of the Trāyastriṃśa gods who, having arrayed himself in robes of various exquisite jewels, descends to this world and then returns to his own abode.

Ajātaśatru has likewise adorned himself with robes and precious jewels; he is like that son of a god descending from above. Although he enters the hell named Piṇḍola, there is no suffering within it—indeed, it would be a hardship [otherwise]—and so the son of a god ascends back to his original place.”
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha: “Excellent!
The transgressions committed by Ajātaśatru have become slight.”
The Buddha asked Śāriputra,
“Do you know who this king is?
He replied:
“I do not know.

“This King Ajātaśatru has made offerings to seventy-three billion Buddhas, and from each of those Buddhas he has constantly heard the profound Dharma; his mind has never been apart from the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
The Buddha again asked Śāriputra:
“Do you see Mañjuśrī? He replied:
“I see it.
“This is the original cause that prompted Ajātaśatru to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Long ago, in the distant past, there was a Buddha named Aninyajñāna (Peaceful Awakening), and the eon was called Vimala (Free from Dust).”
During this kalpa, there were three hundred billion people who were all exhorted by Mañjuśrī to turn the wheel of Dharma.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“It is as if Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were to preach the Dharma to Ajātaśatru, yet he would not resolve his doubts.”
Why is this so? It is because this was the resolve made by Mañjuśrī; one should understand it thus: from lifetime to lifetime, they shall always hear the profound Dharma from Mañjuśrī.
The Buddha said: "A bodhisattva has originally performed certain deeds; that person shall surely attain liberation by virtue of the original resolve they first made.

Although Ajātaśatru has now entered hell, he will subsequently be reborn in the heavens. Five hundred and forty-five world-systems away from here is a land named Vimala-vyūha—'Vimala-vyūha' meaning 'Pure and Adorned' in the language of Han. Its Buddha is named Ratnaketu—'Ratnaketu' meaning 'Jewel-Topknot' in the language of Han. There, he shall encounter Mañjuśrī and, desiring to attend the assembly to hear the Dharma being preached, he will then attain the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)."
At that time, Maitreya will become a Buddha, and Ajātaśatru will come from that land to be born here, at which point he shall be named the Bodhisattva Agaghapi.
For this reason, the Buddha Maitreya will instruct the bodhisattvas through the Dharma; the teachings he proclaims will be neither excessive nor deficient, but perfectly balanced.
At that time, when it is said "Agaghakhi," it refers to King Ajātaśatru during the era of the past Śākyamuni Buddha, who killed his father upon the words of an evil man.
Having heard all dharmas from Mañjuśrī, they rejoiced and attained the patience of acceptance (*kṣānti*); the transgressions they had committed were immediately and completely extinguished.
When Maitreya Buddha spoke these words, eight thousand bodhisattvas all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
After eight *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, Agaghakhi shall practice the bodhisattva path, teaching and transforming sentient beings, and he shall likewise purify a buddha-field.

Any person who hears the Dharma from him—whether they become a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or follow the bodhisattva path—shall all be free from blemish and defilement; all shall be without obstruction, and everyone shall be clear in wisdom and free from doubt.

That King Ajātaśatru shall become a Buddha after the passing of eight asaṃkhyeya kalpas as previously described. That kalpa shall be named *Sukhābhisambodhi* (in Chinese, *Huānxǐjiàn*, meaning "Joyful Vision"); that buddha-field shall be named *Agada* (in Chinese, *Yàowáng*, meaning "Medicine King"), where no sick person fails to be healed; and that Tathāgata shall be titled *Viśuddhasvayaṃbhū* (in Chinese, *Jìngqísùobù*, meaning "Purifier of His Domain").
At that time, when the lifespan is four small kalpas, there will be seven hundred thousand śrāvakas who have all attained liberation through wisdom and shall all know the eight stages of dhyāna.
At that time, there will be twelve billion bodhisattvas, all of whom have entered into various wisdoms and are thoroughly proficient in *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means).
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his Dharma shall remain for as long as a hundred million years before finally coming to an end.
All people in that buddha-field will die without harboring any doubt; after their lives have ended, they shall not be reborn in the eight unfavorable states.
"Why is this? Because they have heard the profound Dharma from the Buddha, no further defilements or turbidities will adhere to them.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"One must not treat a person with contempt. Why is this?
Because by treating them with contempt, one incurs their offense."
The Buddha said:
"I know the deeds performed by humans, yet there is no one else who knows them.
As for their ultimate destination, only a Buddha knows that."
Śāriputra spoke from within that assembly:
"This matter is subtle and profound; it is truly wonderful that you have come to know this.
Then he said:
"From this day forward, I dare not again say that such a person is a sinner or that such a person is a virtuous one. Why is this?
Because the conduct of all people is inconceivable."

When the Buddha had thus explained how Ajātaśatru had received his prediction, at that time twelve thousand devaputras all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, each making the same vow:
"O Śuddhaviśuddha, when you have become a buddha, may we be born in that buddha-field. The Buddha then granted them all their predictions.
"When he attains Buddhahood, you shall be reborn in his subsequent buddha-field.
King Ajātaśatru had a son eight years old named Candanaśrī, who at that moment took the precious jewels from his person and scattered them over the Buddha, saying:
"By this, I resolve my mind upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
"If Śuddhodana Viśvāya becomes a Buddha, I vow to become a Cakravartin King.
After that Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, I vow to succeed him and become a Buddha."

The precious objects thus scattered were all transformed into a pavilion of seven treasures, equal in length and breadth, within which were beds and seats complete with various jewels; its rugs and curtains were likewise so adorned.

The Buddha sat upon his couch; at that moment, the Buddha smiled, and immeasurable rays of light of various colors issued from his mouth, pervading the ten directions, then returned to circle his body three times before entering through the crown of his head.
Ānanda rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha:
"The Tathāgata does not smile without cause; there must be a meaning behind it.
Ānanda then praised the Buddha:

"His wisdom is most sublime and free from all obstructions; he fully knows the mental activities of all people and, according to their inclinations, instructs and illuminates them so that each may find their proper place. Throughout the heavens above and the earth below, he alone is uniquely honored."
Because of the cause and condition for this smile, we only wish to hear it.
