Even if all the people of the ten directions were to stand before you, and each person were to ask hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of questions, you would resolve them all without any hindrance.
Regarding that which you have smiled upon, we have heard only its explanation.

Since the past, the future, and the present, the Buddha has been fully endowed with all-knowledge and is without any obstruction; therefore, regarding that which you have smiled upon, please resolve our doubts.
That radiance completely surpasses the sun and moon and exceeds that of Śakra and Brahmā; it shatters all the Cakravāḍa mountains, causing everyone to see its light.
Those who behold this radiance will no longer have any further attachments.
Why is this? Because the Buddha is free from all defilement.
"Regarding those who laugh at you, I only wish to send them forth.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This Candanaśrī has already made offerings to me and has resolved his mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Gradually arriving there, when Vīśuddha Viśaya attains Buddhahood, he shall be born in that land as a Cakravartin king.
Together with his family, household, and attendants, he shall provide offerings to that Buddha and the community of bhikṣus until the very end, without ceasing.
After that Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, this son shall follow in his succession; then, at the end of his life as a Cakravartin king, he shall go to the Tuṣita heaven.

Descending from the beginning of their lives until the end, they shall be born in that buddha-field and attain buddhahood themselves, with the name Candanaketu. In all respects, they will be no different from the previous buddhas; their lifespans will be exactly equal, and the number of their śrāvakas and bodhisattvas will likewise be equal.
All the other bodhisattvas who had followed Ajātaśatru said:
"In whichever direction Mañjuśrī may be, he is likewise never absent from that place, just as with the Buddha."
Why is this? Because whatever they perform is no different from that of a Buddha.
Any bodhisattva who has been instructed by Mañjuśrī is likewise no longer different [from a Buddha].
Why is this? Because those who are no longer reborn in evil realms do not fear the various Māras, nor do they fear transgressions, and they remain undefiled.

Whether in cities, provinces, kingdoms, districts, towns, villages, or hamlets, if there are those who study this Dharma, or those who write, recite, chant, or read this sutra—upon seeing such persons, one should regard them as no different from the Buddha himself.
"In whatever direction one hears the Dharma, one should then think: 'This is the place where the Buddha resides.
The Buddha said to the bodhisattvas:
"It is exactly as you have said."

Why is this? In the past, incalculable and asankhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Dīpaṃkara who gave me the prediction that I would attain the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and become a Buddha.
I spread my hair upon the ground so that the Tathāgata might tread upon it.
At that very spot, he granted me this prediction:
"After an incalculable number of kalpas have passed, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni."
At that time, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara said to the community of bhikṣus:
"This is the place where the prediction was received; one must not step upon this ground with one's feet. Why is that?
"This is the most supreme and divine place; all devas and humans should together serve this site.
Who would not build a stūpa here?
At that moment, eight billion devas all thought to themselves:
"I shall erect it.
Then there was a householder named Bhadrayaśas, who spoke thus:
"I wish to erect a stūpa here."
He then immediately constructed a stūpa made of the seven precious substances, most magnificently adorned.
When the work was completed, he went to where Dīrghāgama was and said to him:
"The stūpa I have built is finished."
"Having heard of the Tathāgata, what is his merit like?
Ti-wo-chie said:

"If a bodhisattva, wherever he may be, attains the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti), and builds a stūpa as large as a chariot wheel, extending downward to the very limits of the earth, all devas, ghosts, and spirits shall offer worship to it with their respective lands; it shall be no different from a śarīra."

If one were to take a space as large as a chariot wheel—the extent of the ground upon which a bodhisattva receives the prediction of attaining dharma-patience—and fill it with the seven treasures, offering it up to the Buddha from the earth to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
"Whoever builds such a stūpa as this, their merit shall exceed even that.
The Buddha said:
"Just as I have bestowed the prediction upon the Māṇava that he shall later become the Buddha Śākyamuni,"
"By building this stūpa, through this merit, you shall receive a prediction of enlightenment from Śākyamuni Buddha; after incalculable kalpas, you too shall attain Buddhahood."
The Buddha addressed the assembly, saying:
"Do you know the householder Bhadrajyotiṣka?
The members of the assembly did not understand.
The Buddha then said,
"The son of a householder currently present in this assembly, named Karo-yaya-ja, is he.
At that moment, the Tathāgata granted him this prediction.
"You shall become a Buddha, named Sudarśana; in the language of Han, this means 'Decisive Vision'.
The Buddha spoke again:

"If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who write down this sutra, or recite it, read it, or explain its meaning for all people, the area where that Dharma resides will be as vast as a chariot wheel. From the surface of the earth below to the Heaven of the Thirty-three Gods above, it would be filled with dust particles. Suppose a wise person were to take a single particle from among them and offer it in worship."
"Why is this? It is because Bodhisattvas attain patience through these dharmas.
The Buddha said:

"If a man or a woman were to fill a trichiliocosm of Buddha-fields with the seven treasures and offer them as a gift three times every day, while focusing their thoughts exclusively on this [teaching]."
Whatever further deeds they perform— whether for a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas,

or even up to a hundred thousand kalpas— if there are those who recite, read, honor, serve, chant, or explain the "Ajātaśatru Chapter" to all, and who understand the wisdom within it with a mind of unwavering faith and devotion, the merit arising from this surpasses the merit of the aforementioned acts of giving.

If a man or woman were to maintain pure precepts for a hundred kalpas, yet upon finally hearing this Dharma, should believe in it, rejoice in it, and delight in it, their merit would surpass the merit of those pure precepts.
Even if one is beaten, struck, or reviled by others for a hundred kalpas, not to give rise to such thoughts is patience.
To hear this Dharma with faith and inclination, and to practice patience therein, surpasses that [former] patience.

If one were to practice with diligence for a hundred kalpas, respectfully serving all people without regarding it as toil or hardship, and without sparing even their own body or life, yet upon hearing this Dharma,
one believes in it and explains its inner meaning to all people— the merit of the latter exceeds that of the former's diligence.
If one maintains meditative concentration for a hundred kalpas, it is not equal to teaching this Dharma to all people; the merit of the latter exceeds that of maintaining meditative concentration.
If one practices wisdom for a hundred kalpas, yet upon hearing this Dharma realizes that the mind is fundamentally pure, the merit of the latter exceeds that of the former.
All the bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We shall all reverently practice this; wherever we go to the various buddha-fields, we shall transform sentient beings through the Dharma.”
The Buddha said to the bodhisattvas:
"Wherever you go and practice the teachings of the Dharma, all that you do shall be no different from that of a Buddha. Why is this so?"
"This Dharma fully elucidates the affairs of the Buddha.
All the bodhisattvas gathered in the assembly then made offerings of flowers, scattering them over the Tathāgata until they covered the entire trichiliocosm.
Each of the bodhisattvas spoke thus:
"This Dharma is truly supreme.
That which was taught by Śākyamuni Buddha shall remain for a long time in Jambudvīpa and illuminate it."
Mañjuśrī should always remain for a long time.
Why is this? One should always hear from him the profound and wondrous Dharma.
The bodhisattvas said,
"We have yet to offer our bodies, and thus have not repaid their kindness.
The Buddha said:
"If any man or woman hears this Dharma from another, they cannot repay that kindness even with their own bodies.
Those who wish to see the Tathāgata should regard the place where those men or women heard the Dharma as if it were the Buddha himself and offer them worship."
"Whoever has faith in this Dharma should regard such a person as they would the Buddha.
Then the bodhisattvas rose from their seats, paid homage to Śākyamuni Buddha, and suddenly, in a state of trance, they vanished and each returned to his own buddha-field.
By means of this Dharma, he himself, in that very place, fully expounded this wisdom for all.
Those countless people who heard this Dharma all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha said to Maitreya Bodhisattva:

“You should uphold this Dharma by reciting and reading it; you should expound its meaning extensively for the sake of all beings; and you should extend your compassion toward those in the heavens above, the world below, and all others.”
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha:
"I have already heard this Dharma from the presence of past Buddhas and have maintained, recited, and read it.
Now, hearing this Dharma once again, I shall likewise extensively expound this teaching for the sake of all beings."
Even after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, while I am in the Tuṣita Heaven, if there are men or women who wish to study this Dharma, I shall encourage, assist, and protect them.
In the future, at the end of the age when all dharmas are about to perish, wherever this sutra is heard or exists, you should know that it is protected by me.
If there should be Māras who seek to destroy it midway, I shall protect it so that they find no opportunity.
The Buddha said to Śakra-devānām-indra:
"You should uphold this Dharma, recite it, and read it to resolve all doubts.

If the asuras raise an army and mobilize their forces, desiring to attack the Lord of Devas, you should contemplate this sutra; you shall obtain victory immediately, and their armies will be repelled."
The Buddha spoke again:
"If there are commanderies, kingdoms, counties, towns, villages, or hamlets that honor and serve this sutra, you should all go to protect them.
Should those encounter government officials or enter the service of government officials, they should keep this sutra in mind."
When traveling among bandits, one should recollect this sutra; if captured or struck by bandits, one should recollect this sutra.
If in the wilderness, one should recollect this sutra.
If one sees an enemy, or encounters an enemy, one should recollect this sutra.
"Should there be anyone who possesses a sincere mind toward this Dharma, no one shall find an opportunity to harm them.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Uphold this Dharma, recite it, read it, and you should explain and interpret its meaning for the sake of all beings."
If there are men or women who hear this Dharma, they will immediately be free from doubt.

Once all threads of doubt are exhausted, they will no longer be shrouded by transgressions, nor shrouded by birth and death, nor shrouded by abandoning the Dharma midway. All those who would follow false paths shall cease their practice, and they will never encounter the works of Māra.
Why is this so? It is because they have heard this Dharma.

Those who have already committed acts of immediate retribution, upon hearing this Dharma and feeling faith, joy, and delight, will then be free from those acts of immediate retribution and shall no longer undergo the karmic retribution for them.
Mahākāśyapa addressed the Buddha:

“I have realized and witnessed this Dharma. It was when Mañjuśrī was at the meal of Ajātaśatru that he preached this Dharma; it resolved the commission of rebellious and evil deeds, and they immediately attained joyful faith and patience, with all their doubts completely dispelled.”
"I shall now explain this:
those who have committed the heinous crimes of parricide and so forth can all attain liberation through this Dharma-patience, and they too shall be like Ajātaśatru.
At that moment, Mahākāśyapa spoke again:
"All people are fundamentally pure, yet they act contrarily, claiming 'this is mine' or 'this is not mine,' nor do they realize their own fundamental purity.
Those who fully comprehend this fundamental purity are liberated from whatever transgressions they have committed; such are those who understand it as Ajātaśatru does."
"Therefore, all foolish people act in such a way that their deeds turn back upon them and destroy their own bodies; they thereby encounter toil and suffering and enter hell.
Mahākāśyapa said, "Those who honor, serve, believe in, and delight in this Dharma—we ourselves bear witness—that they shall no longer fall into the evil realms."
The Buddha said, “It is as you have said.
The minds of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are free from blemish and defilement.”
Ānanda again addressed the Buddha:
“May the Tathāgata cause future generations to behold this Dharma.
At that moment, the Tathāgata emitted light from the marks of his body, illuminating countless Buddha-fields; from all the walls and trees there arose sounds:
"It is the nature of that Dharma. Why is this?
If the fire at the end of the kalpa were to arise, those who are to hear it would still be present; such is the nature of that Dharma."
"If they were to hear this Dharma, even though they were in the midst of the ocean, they would still be able to hear it.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"It is exactly as you have heard regarding the sounds from walls and trees; it is indeed as you have described."
"Those who have already performed meritorious deeds and have already practiced the Mahāyāna shall all, in future lives, again hear this Dharma.

While this sutra was being preached, ninety-six thousand devas and humans all attained the stage of Srotāpanna; seventy-eight thousand people all resolved their minds toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; two thousand bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); and eight thousand people all attained the path of Arhatship.
This trichiliocosm shook in six ways; all darkness was dispelled and everything became bright.
The sons of the gods from the desire realm and the form realm made offerings with various kinds of music, scattering celestial flowers and celestial incense together, saying:
"That which is called the Wheel of Dharma—those who hear this Dharma have already attained the turning of the Wheel of Dharma."
When the various non-Buddhists hear this Dharma, they immediately realize it for themselves.
Therefore, the seal that subdues them is the Bodhisattva Seal; those who obtain this seal shall reach the foot of the Bodhi tree.

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, King Ajātaśatru, the various bodhisattvas—of whom Mañjuśrī was the foremost—and the various śrāvakas—of whom Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Ānanda, and others were the foremost—as well as all the devas, gandharvas, and humans, having heard what the Buddha taught, came forward, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and departed.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on King Ajātaśatru, Scroll II.
